cs-u3-q08.hint: Try making the final conclusion \(\mathrm{false}\) while keeping the premises \(\mathrm{true}\).
cs-u3-q08.explanation: With \(P=\mathrm{false}\) and \(Q=\mathrm{true}\), \(P\Rightarrow Q\) and \(Q\) are both \(\mathrm{true}\), but \(P\) is \(\mathrm{false}\). This is the invalid inference of affirming the consequent.
solutionSteps: With \(P=\mathrm{false}\) and \(Q=\mathrm{true}\), \(P\Rightarrow Q\) and \(Q\) are both \(\mathrm{true}\), but \(P\) is \(\mathrm{false}\). This is the invalid inference of affirming the consequent.

cs-u3-q09.title: Read CNF
cs-u3-q09.statement: Which expression is written as an AND of OR-clauses of literals?
cs-u3-q09.hint: Inspect the outermost operation, then each clause.
cs-u3-q09.explanation: B is syntactically CNF: two OR-clauses joined by AND. A is DNF. C has a negation applied to a compound expression.
solutionSteps: B is syntactically CNF: two OR-clauses joined by AND. A is DNF. C has a negation applied to a compound expression.

cs-u3-q10.title: Select two true rows
cs-u3-q10.statement: Over variables \(P\),\(Q\), a formula is \(\mathrm{true}\) exactly at \((\mathrm{false},\mathrm{false})\) and \((\mathrm{true},\mathrm{false})\). Which is its full DNF, with a term for each \(\mathrm{true}\) row?
cs-u3-q10.hint: Each term must be \(\mathrm{true}\) on exactly its own row.
cs-u3-q10.explanation: Both desired rows have \(Q=\mathrm{false}\), so both terms contain \(\neg Q\). Their \(P\) literals select the two different values of \(P\). The expression simplifies to \(\neg Q\).
solutionSteps: Both desired rows have \(Q=\mathrm{false}\), so both terms contain \(\neg Q\). Their \(P\) literals select the two different values of \(P\). The expression simplifies to \(\neg Q\).

cs-u3-q11.title: Distribute OR over AND
cs-u3-q11.statement: Which CNF is equivalent to \(P \lor  (Q \land  R)\)?
cs-u3-q11.explanation: OR distributes over AND in Boolean algebra. If \(P\) is \(\mathrm{true}\) both clauses hold; if \(P\) is \(\mathrm{false}\) both \(Q\) and \(R\) are required.
solutionSteps: OR distributes over AND in Boolean algebra. If \(P\) is \(\mathrm{true}\) both clauses hold; if \(P\) is \(\mathrm{false}\) both \(Q\) and \(R\) are required.

cs-u3-q12.title: Count the rows
cs-u3-q12.statement: A truth table includes seven independent Boolean variables. How many assignments must a full table list? Enter an integer.
cs-u3-q12.hint: Double the row count whenever another Boolean variable is added.
cs-u3-q12.explanation: Each of the seven variables has two choices, giving \(2^{7}=128\) assignments. This counts rows, not the total cost of evaluating every formula on them.
solutionSteps: Each of the seven variables has two choices, giving \(2^{7}=128\) assignments. This counts rows, not the total cost of evaluating every formula on them.

cs-u3-q13.title: Find a consistent configuration
cs-u3-q13.statement: Which assignment satisfies \((P \lor  Q) \land  (\neg P \lor  R) \land  \neg R\)?
cs-u3-q13.hint: Start with the single-literal constraint \(\neg R\).
cs-u3-q13.explanation: \(\neg R\) forces \(R=\mathrm{false}\). Then \(\neg P\lor R\) forces \(P=\mathrm{false}\), and \(P\lor Q\) forces \(Q=\mathrm{true}\). C is the unique satisfying assignment.
solutionSteps: \(\neg R\) forces \(R=\mathrm{false}\). Then \(\neg P\lor R\) forces \(P=\mathrm{false}\), and \(P\lor Q\) forces \(Q=\mathrm{true}\). C is the unique satisfying assignment.

cs-u3-q14.title: Explain an impossibility
cs-u3-q14.statement: Why is \((A \lor  B) \land  \neg A \land  \neg B\) unsatisfiable?
cs-u3-q14.hint: Apply the two single-literal constraints to the remaining clause.
cs-u3-q14.explanation: \(\neg A\) and \(\neg B\) require both variables to be \(\mathrm{false}\), leaving no way to satisfy \(A\lor B\). Negations and clause counts alone say nothing about satisfiability.
solutionSteps: \(\neg A\) and \(\neg B\) require both variables to be \(\mathrm{false}\), leaving no way to satisfy \(A\lor B\). Negations and clause counts alone say nothing about satisfiability.

options.a: The final two constraints force the first one to be \(\mathrm{false}\)
options.b: Any formula with negations is unsatisfiable
options.c: It has an odd number of clauses

cs-u3-q15.title: Use SAT to check validity
cs-u3-q15.statement: A sound SAT solver reports that \(\neg F\) is unsatisfiable. What follows?
cs-u3-q15.hint: Translate “no satisfying assignment for \(\neg F\)” into a statement about \(F\).
cs-u3-q15.explanation: There is no assignment on which \(\neg F\) is \(\mathrm{true}\), so none on which \(F\) is \(\mathrm{false}\). That is validity, not uniqueness.
solutionSteps: There is no assignment on which \(\neg F\) is \(\mathrm{true}\), so none on which \(F\) is \(\mathrm{false}\). That is validity, not uniqueness.

cs-u3-q16.title: What a failed trial proves
cs-u3-q16.statement: A candidate assignment makes one of a system’\(s\) constraints \(\mathrm{false}\). What has been established?
cs-u3-q16.hint: The SAT question uses “there exists,” not “this particular assignment.”
cs-u3-q16.explanation: The trial rejects one candidate only. Other assignments may satisfy every constraint; rejecting all of them requires further reasoning.
solutionSteps: The trial rejects one candidate only. Other assignments may satisfy every constraint; rejecting all of them requires further reasoning.

options.c: This assignment is not a witness; the system may still be satisfiable

cs-u3-q17.title: Only enabled jobs
cs-u3-q17.statement: Let J be all jobs; \(E(j)\) means enabled and \(R(j)\) means ready. Which formula says “Every enabled job is ready”?
cs-u3-q17.hint: A disabled job must not automatically violate the statement.
cs-u3-q17.explanation: The implication imposes readiness only on enabled jobs. B also requires all jobs to be enabled; C does not establish a universal condition.
solutionSteps: The implication imposes readiness only on enabled jobs. B also requires all jobs to be enabled; C does not establish a universal condition.

cs-u3-q18.title: An existential restriction
cs-u3-q18.statement: Which formula says “At least one job is both enabled and ready”?
cs-u3-q18.hint: The witness must actually be enabled.
cs-u3-q18.explanation: The same witness must satisfy both properties. An existential implication could instead be witnessed by a disabled job.
solutionSteps: The same witness must satisfy both properties. An existential implication could instead be witnessed by a disabled job.

cs-u3-q19.title: Empty batch
cs-u3-q19.statement: For an empty job set J, what are the truth values of \(\forall j\in J R(j)\) and \(\exists j\in J R(j)\), in that order?
cs-u3-q19.hint: Look separately for a violating element and a satisfying element.
cs-u3-q19.explanation: There is no counterexample to the universal claim and no witness for the existential claim. An empty batch therefore passes an all-items condition but not an any-item condition.
solutionSteps: There is no counterexample to the universal claim and no witness for the existential claim. An empty batch therefore passes an all-items condition but not an any-item condition.

cs-u3-q20.title: Domain changes truth
cs-u3-q20.statement: Compare \(\exists x\in Z\,(2x=1)\) with \(\exists x\in R\,(2x=1)\). Which statement is correct?
cs-u3-q20.hint: Solving the equation is not enough; check where the solution belongs.
cs-u3-q20.explanation: The unique real solution \(\frac{1}{2}\) is not an integer. A witness is valid only if it belongs to the stated domain.
solutionSteps: The unique real solution \(\frac{1}{2}\) is not an integer. A witness is valid only if it belongs to the stated domain.

options.a: The integer claim is \(\mathrm{false}\); the real claim is \(\mathrm{true}\)

cs-u3-q21.title: Per-query indexes
cs-u3-q21.statement: \(I(q,i)\) means index \(i\) supports query \(q\). Which statement permits different queries to use different indexes?
cs-u3-q21.hint: Which choice is allowed to depend on the other?
cs-u3-q21.explanation: B chooses an index after the query is fixed. A demands one common index; C demands every index support every query.
solutionSteps: B chooses an index after the query is fixed. A demands one common index; C demands every index support every query.

cs-u3-q22.title: Inspect a finite model
cs-u3-q22.statement: Let \(Q=\{a,b\}\), \(I=\{1,2\}\). \(I(q,i)\) holds exactly for \((a,1)\) and \((b,2)\). What is \(\mathrm{true}\)?
cs-u3-q22.hint: Check both rows for per-query witnesses, then each column for a common witness.
cs-u3-q22.explanation: Choose \(1\) for a and \(2\) for \(b\). Index \(1\) fails for \(b\), and index \(2\) fails for a; those are all available indexes.
solutionSteps: Choose \(1\) for a and \(2\) for \(b\). Index \(1\) fails for \(b\), and index \(2\) fails for a; those are all available indexes.

options.a: There is one index supporting all queries
options.c: Every query has an index, but no index supports all queries

cs-u3-q23.title: An implication that always works
cs-u3-q23.statement: For nonempty sets A,B and any relation \(R\), which implication is always \(\mathrm{true}\)?
cs-u3-q23.hint: Reuse the common witness instead of choosing a new one.
cs-u3-q23.explanation: A single common \(y\) can be reused for every \(x\). Separate witnesses need not coincide, as the two-query model shows.
solutionSteps: A single common \(y\) can be reused for every \(x\). Separate witnesses need not coincide, as the two-query model shows.

options.a: \((\exists y\in B \forall x\in A R(x,y)) \Rightarrow  (\forall x\in A \exists y\in B R(x,y))\)
options.b: \((\forall x\in A \exists y\in B R(x,y)) \Rightarrow  (\exists y\in B \forall x\in A R(x,y))\)

cs-u3-q24.title: An integer witness
cs-u3-q24.statement: Which function \(y(x)\) supplies a witness for \(\forall x\in Z \exists y\in Z\,(y>x)\)?
cs-u3-q24.hint: A witness rule must work for negative and positive \(x\) alike.
cs-u3-q24.explanation: For every integer \(x\), \(x+1\) is an integer strictly larger than \(x\). Zero fails when \(x\ge 0\), and \(x-1\) is always smaller.
solutionSteps: For every integer \(x\), \(x+1\) is an integer strictly larger than \(x\). Zero fails when \(x\ge 0\), and \(x-1\) is always smaller.

cs-u3-q25.title: Negate a bounded rule
cs-u3-q25.hint: First negate the universal quantifier, then the implication.
cs-u3-q25.explanation: One enabled, unsafe job refutes the universal implication. It is unnecessary for all jobs to be unsafe, and a disabled job is irrelevant.
solutionSteps: One enabled, unsafe job refutes the universal implication. It is unnecessary for all jobs to be unsafe, and a disabled job is irrelevant.

cs-u3-q26.title: No universal test
cs-u3-q26.hint: Keep the original variable order while swapping each quantifier.
cs-u3-q26.explanation: Every candidate test must miss at least one bug; the missed bug may depend on the test. B is too weak, and C changes quantifier order.
solutionSteps: Every candidate test must miss at least one bug; the missed bug may depend on the test. B is too weak, and C changes quantifier order.

cs-u3-q27.title: One witness cannot be split
cs-u3-q27.statement: The claim “\((\exists x\in D P(x)) \land  (\exists x\in D Q(x))\) implies \(\exists x\in D\,(P(x) \land  Q(x))\)” is proposed. Which interpretation refutes it?
cs-u3-q27.hint: The two existential witnesses need not be the same element.
cs-u3-q27.explanation: Each predicate has a witness in B, so the premise is \(\mathrm{true}\). No element satisfies both, so the conclusion is \(\mathrm{false}\). A and C satisfy the conclusion.
solutionSteps: Each predicate has a witness in B, so the premise is \(\mathrm{true}\). No element satisfies both, so the conclusion is \(\mathrm{false}\). A and C satisfy the conclusion.

options.b: \(D=\{a,b\}\); \(P\) holds only at a and \(Q\) only at \(b\)

cs-u3-q28.title: Certify a coverage failure
cs-u3-q28.statement: A specification is \(\forall r\,\in\)Requests \(\exists s\in \mathrm{Servers}\,\operatorname{Handles}(r,s)\). Which evidence suffices to refute it?
cs-u3-q28.hint: Negate the full quantified statement before choosing the evidence.
cs-u3-q28.explanation: A bad pair may be covered by another server. An unused server may be irrelevant. One request with no working server is exactly the negation of the specification.
solutionSteps: A bad pair may be covered by another server. An unused server may be irrelevant. One request with no working server is exactly the negation of the specification.

options.b: One server that handles no requests
options.c: One request for which every server fails Handles

cs-u4-q01.title: Deduplicate a collection
cs-u4-q01.statement: How many elements are in \(\{\mathrm{api}, \mathrm{worker}, \mathrm{api}, \mathrm{cache}, \mathrm{worker}\}\)? Enter an integer.
cs-u4-q01.hint: Count distinct objects, not positions in the listing.
cs-u4-q01.explanation: The distinct elements are api, worker and cache. Repeated occurrences in a set listing do not add elements.
solutionSteps: The distinct elements are api, worker and cache. Repeated occurrences in a set listing do not add elements.

cs-u4-q02.title: A set containing an empty set
cs-u4-q02.hint: Membership and subset inclusion ask different questions.
cs-u4-q02.explanation: \(S\) contains the two distinct sets \(\varnothing \) and \(\{x\}\). The empty set is one of its elements and is also a subset, since it has no elements that could violate inclusion.
solutionSteps: \(S\) contains the two distinct sets \(\varnothing \) and \(\{x\}\). The empty set is one of its elements and is also a subset, since it has no elements that could violate inclusion.

cs-u4-q03.title: Read a set-builder filter
cs-u4-q03.statement: Let \(D=\{0,1,2,3,4,5,6\}\). Which set equals \(\{x\in D \mid  x \text{is even and} x<5\}\)?
cs-u4-q03.hint: Apply the predicate to the whole domain, including zero.
cs-u4-q03.explanation: Zero is even and satisfies \(0<5\). Six is even but fails the strict upper bound. Each element must satisfy both conditions.
solutionSteps: Zero is even and satisfies \(0<5\). Six is even but fails the strict upper bound. Each element must satisfy both conditions.

cs-u4-q04.title: Member of a power set
cs-u4-q04.statement: Let \(A=\{\mathrm{read},\mathrm{write}\}\). Which object is an element of \(\operatorname{pow}(A)\)?
cs-u4-q04.hint: A power set contains sets, not the underlying labels directly.
cs-u4-q04.explanation: An element of \(\operatorname{pow}(A)\) must itself be a subset of A. \(\{\mathrm{read}\}\) is such a subset; read is a label rather than that subset, and execute is not in A.
solutionSteps: An element of \(\operatorname{pow}(A)\) must itself be a subset of A. \(\{\mathrm{read}\}\) is such a subset; read is a label rather than that subset, and execute is not in A.

cs-u4-q05.title: Filter eligible users
cs-u4-q05.statement: Let \(\operatorname{Enabled}=\{a,b,c\}\), Suspended=\(\{b,d\}\), and Premium=\(\{b,c,d\}\). Which set is (Enabled\Suspended)\(\cap\)Premium?
cs-u4-q05.hint: Perform the difference before the intersection.
cs-u4-q05.explanation: Removing suspended users from Enabled leaves \(\{a,c\}\); intersecting with Premium leaves only \(c\).
solutionSteps: Removing suspended users from Enabled leaves \(\{a,c\}\); intersecting with Premium leaves only \(c\).

cs-u4-q06.title: Complement needs a universe
cs-u4-q06.statement: Let \(A=\{1,3\}\). Its complement is computed in \(U=\{0,1,2,3,4\}\). Which result is correct?
cs-u4-q06.explanation: The complement includes precisely the members of \(U\) not in A. A larger universe would generally give a different complement.
solutionSteps: The complement includes precisely the members of \(U\) not in A. A larger universe would generally give a different complement.

cs-u4-q07.title: Complete an equality proof
cs-u4-q07.statement: For arbitrary \(x\), \(x\in A\setminus (B\cup C)\) iff \(x\in A\) and \(x\notin B\) and \(x\notin C\). Which set has exactly that membership condition?
cs-u4-q07.hint: “And” between two membership conditions corresponds to intersection.
cs-u4-q07.explanation: Membership in both differences requires membership in A and exclusion from both B and C. This equivalence proves the equality for every element.
solutionSteps: Membership in both differences requires membership in A and exclusion from both B and C. This equivalence proves the equality for every element.

cs-u4-q08.title: Refute a false identity
cs-u4-q08.statement: Someone claims \(A\setminus (B\cap C)\)=(\(A\setminus B\))\(\cap\)(\(A\setminus C\)) for all sets. Which choice disproves it?
cs-u4-q08.hint: Seek an element lying in exactly one of B and C.
cs-u4-q08.explanation: For C’\(s\) choice, \(B\cap C=\varnothing \), so the left side is \(\{x\}\). The right side is \(\varnothing \cap \{x\}=\varnothing \). The other two choices make both sides empty.
solutionSteps: For C’\(s\) choice, \(B\cap C=\varnothing \), so the left side is \(\{x\}\). The right side is \(\varnothing \cap \{x\}=\varnothing \). The other two choices make both sides empty.

cs-u4-q09.title: Set versus sequence
cs-u4-q09.statement: Let \(s=(2,2,5)\) and \(A=\{2,2,5\}\). What are \(\operatorname{length}(s)\) and \(\lvert A\rvert \), respectively?
cs-u4-q09.hint: Sequences count positions; sets count distinct elements.
cs-u4-q09.explanation: The sequence has three positions, including two equal components. The set has only the distinct elements \(2\) and \(5\).
solutionSteps: The sequence has three positions, including two equal components. The set has only the distinct elements \(2\) and \(5\).

cs-u4-q10.title: Check a product type
cs-u4-q10.statement: Let \(E=\{\mathrm{prod},\mathrm{stage}\}\) and \(P=\{80,443\}\). Which is a member of \(E\times P\)?
cs-u4-q10.hint: Check both the container type and the order of its components.
cs-u4-q10.explanation: The first component must belong to E and the second to \(P\). A reverses their types; C is an unordered set, not a pair.
solutionSteps: The first component must belong to E and the second to \(P\). A reverses their types; C is an unordered set, not a pair.

cs-u4-q11.title: An impossible component
cs-u4-q11.statement: How many elements are in \(\{\mathrm{GET},\mathrm{POST}\}\times \varnothing \)? Enter an integer.
cs-u4-q11.hint: Can you choose the second component?
cs-u4-q11.explanation: A pair in the product needs a second component from \(\varnothing \). No such component exists, so the product is empty.
solutionSteps: A pair in the product needs a second component from \(\varnothing \). No such component exists, so the product is empty.

cs-u4-q12.title: The zero-length case
cs-u4-q12.statement: How many sequences are in \(\{0,1\}^{0}\)? Enter an integer.
cs-u4-q12.hint: Distinguish the empty sequence from an empty collection of sequences.
cs-u4-q12.explanation: There is exactly one length-zero sequence: the empty sequence. This is different from having no sequences at all.
solutionSteps: There is exactly one length-zero sequence: the empty sequence. This is different from having no sequences at all.

cs-u4-q13.title: A precise lookup model
cs-u4-q13.statement: Let \(A=\{a,b,c\}\) and \(B=\{0,1\}\). A lookup has graph \(\{(a,0),(b,1)\}\) and no other pairs. Which description is correct?
cs-u4-q13.hint: At most one output and exactly one output are different conditions.
cs-u4-q13.explanation: Each input has at most one output, so it is a function under the book’\(s\) convention. It is not total on A because \(c\) has no output.
solutionSteps: Each input has at most one output, so it is a function under the book’\(s\) convention. It is not total on A because \(c\) has no output.

options.b: Not a function because \(c\) has no value
options.c: A partial function with support \(\{a,b\}\) and range \(\{0,1\}\)

cs-u4-q14.title: Range is not codomain
cs-u4-q14.statement: Let \(f:\{0,1,2,3\}\to \{0,1,2\}\) be the total function \(f(x)=x \bmod  2\). What is its range?
cs-u4-q14.hint: Evaluate the mapping on its four inputs.
cs-u4-q14.explanation: The only produced values are \(0\) and \(1\). The value \(2\) is allowed by the codomain but never occurs.
solutionSteps: The only produced values are \(0\) and \(1\). The value \(2\) is allowed by the codomain but never occurs.

cs-u4-q15.title: Compose two transformations
cs-u4-q15.statement: Let \(f\),\(g:Z\to Z\) be total, with \(f(x)=2x-1\) and \(g(x)=x+4\). Find \((g\circ f)(3)\). Enter an integer.
cs-u4-q15.hint: Read \(g\circ f\) from right to left when evaluating an input.
cs-u4-q15.explanation: First \(f(3)=5\), then \(g(5)=9\). Applying the maps in the opposite order would give \(f(7)=13\).
solutionSteps: First \(f(3)=5\), then \(g(5)=9\). Applying the maps in the opposite order would give \(f(7)=13\).

cs-u4-q16.title: Composition can lose support
cs-u4-q16.statement: Let \(f:\{a,b\}\to \{0,1\}\) have \(f(a)=0\), \(f(b)=1\). Let \(g:\{0,1\}\to Z\) be defined only by \(g(1)=7\). What is \(\operatorname{support}(g\circ f)\)?
cs-u4-q16.hint: The intermediate value must be a supported input of \(g\).
cs-u4-q16.explanation: The composite is undefined at a because \(g(0)\) is undefined. At \(b\) it is defined and equals \(7\).
solutionSteps: The composite is undefined at a because \(g(0)\) is undefined. At \(b\) it is defined and equals \(7\).

cs-u4-q17.title: A many-valued relation
cs-u4-q17.statement: Let \(R\) go from \(A=\{a,b\}\) to \(B=\{1,2,3\}\), with graph \(\{(a,1),(a,2),(b,3)\}\). Which description is correct?
cs-u4-q17.hint: Count outgoing and incoming pairs separately; use the book’\(s\) relation terminology.
cs-u4-q17.explanation: Every input has an output, every output is reached, and none has two incoming inputs. But a has two outputs, so \(R\) is not functional and hence not bijective.
solutionSteps: Every input has an output, every output is reached, and none has two incoming inputs. But a has two outputs, so \(R\) is not functional and hence not bijective.

options.a: Total, injective and surjective, but not a function
options.c: A function that is not total

cs-u4-q18.title: A collision
cs-u4-q18.statement: A total function \(f:\{a,b,c\}\to \{0,1\}\) has \(f(a)=0\), \(f(b)=1\), \(f(c)=1\). Which property fails?
cs-u4-q18.hint: Look for two different inputs with the same output.
cs-u4-q18.explanation: Distinct inputs \(b\) and \(c\) share output \(1\). Both outputs are reached and every input has exactly one value, so the other properties hold.
solutionSteps: Distinct inputs \(b\) and \(c\) share output \(1\). Both outputs are reached and every input has exactly one value, so the other properties hold.

cs-u4-q19.title: Same graph, different codomain
cs-u4-q19.statement: The graph \(\{(a,1),(b,2)\}\) is used first with codomain \(\{1,2\}\), then with codomain \(\{1,2,3\}\). The domain stays \(\{a,b\}\). What changes?
cs-u4-q19.hint: A codomain includes allowed values even when the graph does not reach them.
cs-u4-q19.explanation: The additional codomain element \(3\) has no incoming pair. Input coverage and uniqueness of outputs are unchanged.
solutionSteps: The additional codomain element \(3\) has no incoming pair. Input coverage and uniqueness of outputs are unchanged.

options.a: The mapping ceases to be a function

cs-u4-q20.title: Recognize a bijection
cs-u4-q20.statement: For \(A=\{a,b,c\}\) and \(B=\{1,2,3\}\), which graph defines a bijection?
cs-u4-q20.hint: Check exactly one outgoing and exactly one incoming pair at every endpoint.
cs-u4-q20.explanation: C gives each input exactly one output and reaches each output exactly once. A has a collision and misses \(2\); B leaves \(c\) unsupported and misses \(3\).
solutionSteps: C gives each input exactly one output and reaches each output exactly once. A has a collision and misses \(2\); B leaves \(c\) unsupported and misses \(3\).

cs-u4-q21.title: Compute an image
cs-u4-q21.statement: Let \(f:\{a,b,c,d\}\to \{0,1,2\}\) be total with values \(0\),\(1\),\(1\),\(2\) respectively. What is \(f(\{b,c,d\})\)?
cs-u4-q21.hint: An image is a set of outputs.
cs-u4-q21.explanation: The image is the set of values produced by \(b\),\(c\),\(d: 1\),\(1\),\(2\). Repetition contributes no new element, so the result is \(\{1,2\}\). Zero is produced only by a, which is not in the input subset.
solutionSteps: The image is the set of values produced by \(b\),\(c\),\(d: 1\),\(1\),\(2\). Repetition contributes no new element, so the result is \(\{1,2\}\). Zero is produced only by a, which is not in the input subset.

cs-u4-q22.title: Compute a preimage
cs-u4-q22.hint: Collect all inputs whose output is \(1\).
cs-u4-q22.explanation: Both \(b\) and \(c\) map to a value in \(\{1\}\). A preimage includes every such input and need not be a singleton.
solutionSteps: Both \(b\) and \(c\) map to a value in \(\{1\}\). A preimage includes every such input and need not be a singleton.

cs-u4-q23.title: Reverse a collision
cs-u4-q23.statement: Let \(f:\{a,b\}\to \{0\}\) be total with \(f(a)=f(b)=0\). Is its inverse relation a function under the book’\(s\) at-most-one-output convention?
cs-u4-q23.hint: Reverse the pairs and inspect outgoing values.
cs-u4-q23.explanation: Reversing the two pairs gives \((0,a)\) and \((0,b)\). One input now has two distinct outputs, violating functionality.
solutionSteps: Reversing the two pairs gives \((0,a)\) and \((0,b)\). One input now has two distinct outputs, violating functionality.

options.c: No, because \(0\) is related to both a and \(b\)

cs-u4-q24.title: Preimage respects intersection
cs-u4-q24.statement: Let \(f:A\to B\) be a total function and \(X\),\(Y\subseteq B\). Which equality holds for all such \(X\),Y?
cs-u4-q24.hint: Translate membership in the left side into two conditions on \(f(a)\).
cs-u4-q24.explanation: An input belongs on the left iff its single output belongs to both \(X\) and Y, which is exactly membership in both preimages. Inputs and outputs may have different types, so C is not generally meaningful as an equality.

solutionSteps: Inorder traversal of any valid search tree with distinct keys lists them in increasing order, here \(4\),\(7\),\(10\),\(15\). The recursive bounds put every left-subtree key before its root and every right-subtree key after it.

cs-u8-q06.statement: Someone proposes listing \(N^{2}\) by outputting \((0,0)\),\((0,1)\),\((0,2)\),... and, after finishing that row, starting \((1,0)\),\((1,1)\),... . What fails?

solutionSteps: The pair \((a,b)\) belongs to diagonal \(a+b\). Only finitely many diagonals precede it, and diagonal \(k\) has \(k+1\) pairs. Its own position within its diagonal is also finite.

options.b: Every pair has finitely many predecessors because every earlier diagonal is finite
options.c: Every pair occurs on infinitely many diagonals

cs-u8-q08.title: Handle duplicate fractions
cs-u8-q08.statement: A diagonal enumeration of positive numerator-denominator pairs outputs \(\frac{1}{2}\) and later \(\frac{2}{4}\). Does this invalidate the proof that the positive rationals are countable?

solutionSteps: A surjection from \(N\) onto a nonempty set establishes countability. Fraction representations need not be unique; every positive rational still has a positive numerator and denominator.

options.a: Yes; a surjective listing must also be injective
options.b: Yes; equal fractions prove there are uncountably many rationals
options.c: No; every positive rational is reached, and duplicate values may be skipped if a distinct listing is wanted

cs-u8-q14.title: Identify the contradiction
cs-u8-q14.statement: For arbitrary total \(g:A\to P(A)\), set \(D=\{a\in A:a\notin g(a)\}\). If \(D=g(t)\) for some \(t\in A\), what follows?

solutionSteps: By definition, \(t\in D\) iff \(t\notin g(t)\). Substituting \(g(t)=D\) gives a proposition equivalent to its own negation, so the assumed preimage \(t\) cannot exist.

cs-u9-q32.title: Repair the all-message proof
cs-u9-q32.statement: For this toy key, ed=\(145\). The message \(m=7\) is not coprime to \(n=91\), so Euler modulo \(91\) cannot be applied directly. Which argument still proves \(m^{145}\equiv m\,(\bmod  91)\)?

cs-u9-q32.explanation: Modulo \(7\), \(7^{145}\) and \(7\) are both \(0\). Modulo \(13\), \(7^{145}=7\cdot (7^{12})^{12}\equiv 7\). Hence their difference is divisible by \(7\) and by \(13\), and therefore by \(91\). The general proof similarly separates zero and nonzero residues for each prime.
