ml-lr-q07.title: Change the objective
ml-lr-q07.hint: Add absolute residuals rather than their squares.
ml-lr-q07.explanation: \(\mathrm{MAE}_A=\frac{4}{3}\); \(\mathrm{MAE}_B=\frac{6}{3}=2\). A wins under \(\mathrm{MAE}\), while B won under squared loss. Choosing an objective changes how errors are penalized; neither batch metric alone proves better generalization.
solutionSteps: \(\mathrm{MAE}_A=\frac{4}{3}\); \(\mathrm{MAE}_B=\frac{6}{3}=2\). A wins under \(\mathrm{MAE}\), while B won under squared loss. Choosing an objective changes how errors are penalized; neither batch metric alone proves better generalization.

ml-gd-q05.title: Find the bias gradient
ml-gd-q05.prompt: What is the full-batch bias gradient? Enter an integer.
ml-gd-q05.hint: Average the residuals at the current parameters.
ml-gd-q05.explanation: Predictions are \(1\) and \(3\), so residuals are \(-1\) and \(1\). The bias gradient is \(\frac{-1+1}{2}=0\). The weight gradient can still be nonzero.
solutionSteps: Predictions are \(1\) and \(3\), so residuals are \(-1\) and \(1\). The bias gradient is \(\frac{-1+1}{2}=0\). The weight gradient can still be nonzero.

ml-gd-q06.title: Update the weight
ml-gd-q06.statement:
Model: \(\hat y=b+wx\); \((b,w)=(0,1)\).
Batch (\(x\),\(y\)): \((1,2)\), \((3,2)\).
Half-\(\mathrm{MSE}\): \(L=\frac{1}{2n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(b+wx_i-y_i)^2\); \(n\) = \(2\).
Full-batch simultaneous update: \(\alpha=\frac{1}{2}\).
ml-gd-q06.hint: Average residual times \(x\), then subtract \(\alpha\) times that gradient.
ml-gd-q06.explanation: At the old parameters, residuals are \(-1\) and \(1\). The weight gradient is \(\frac{(-1)\cdot1+1\cdot3}{2}=1\). Thus \(w_{\mathrm{new}}=1-\frac{1}{2}\cdot1=\frac{1}{2}\); the bias remains \(0\). Omitting the average gives \(0\); adding the gradient gives \(\frac{3}{2}\).
solutionSteps: At the old parameters, residuals are \(-1\) and \(1\). The weight gradient is \(\frac{(-1)\cdot1+1\cdot3}{2}=1\). Thus \(w_{\mathrm{new}}=1-\frac{1}{2}\cdot1=\frac{1}{2}\); the bias remains \(0\). Omitting the average gives \(0\); adding the gradient gives \(\frac{3}{2}\).

ml-gd-q07.title: Will it converge?
ml-gd-q07.explanation: The error multiplier is \(-1\), so the error changes sign without shrinking. Starting at \(0\) gives \(0\), \(6\), \(0\), \(6\), ... . Convexity does not guarantee convergence for every step size. Starting exactly at \(3\) would stay there.
solutionSteps: The error multiplier is \(-1\), so the error changes sign without shrinking. Starting at \(0\) gives \(0\), \(6\), \(0\), \(6\), ... . Convexity does not guarantee convergence for every step size. Starting exactly at \(3\) would stay there.

ml-gd-q08.title: Increase the step size
ml-gd-q08.statement:
Same loss: \(L(\theta)=2(\theta-3)^2\).
Exact gradient descent: \(\theta_0=0\), fixed \(\alpha=\frac{3}{5}\).
ml-gd-q08.prompt: What happens to the distance from \(3\)?
ml-gd-q08.explanation: The error multiplier is \(1-\frac{12}{5}=-\frac{7}{5}\). Since its magnitude exceeds \(1\), the nonzero starting error alternates in sign and grows without bound. In contrast, \(\alpha=\frac{1}{4}\) makes the multiplier zero and reaches \(3\) in one step.
solutionSteps: The error multiplier is \(1-\frac{12}{5}=-\frac{7}{5}\). Since its magnitude exceeds \(1\), the nonzero starting error alternates in sign and grows without bound. In contrast, \(\alpha=\frac{1}{4}\) makes the multiplier zero and reaches \(3\) in one step.

ml-logistic-q01.title: Turn a score into a probability
ml-logistic-q01.prompt: What probability does it predict? Enter a decimal.
ml-logistic-q01.explanation: \(p=1/(1+1/3)=3/4=0.75\). This is a model probability, not a guarantee that the event occurs.
solutionSteps: \(p=1/(1+1/3)=3/4=0.75\). This is a model probability, not a guarantee that the event occurs.

ml-logistic-q02.title: Interpret a feature weight
ml-logistic-q02.statement: A logistic model has \(w_j=\ln 2\). Increase \(x_j\) by 1 and hold every other feature fixed.
ml-logistic-q02.hint: The linear score is the log of the odds.
ml-logistic-q02.explanation: The score increases by \(\ln 2\), so odds are multiplied by \(e^{\ln 2}=2\). For example, odds 1 become 2: probability changes from \(1/2\) to \(2/3\), not to 1.
solutionSteps: The score increases by \(\ln 2\), so odds are multiplied by \(e^{\ln 2}=2\). For example, odds 1 become 2: probability changes from \(1/2\) to \(2/3\), not to 1.

ml-logistic-q03.title: A confidently wrong prediction
ml-logistic-q03.statement: The true label is \(y=0\), but the model predicts \(p=0.9\). Use natural-log cross-entropy.
ml-logistic-q03.prompt: What is the loss for this example?
ml-logistic-q03.hint: Use the probability assigned to the true label, which is class 0.
ml-logistic-q03.explanation: The loss is \(-\ln(1-0.9)=-\ln(0.1)=\ln 10\). A confident wrong prediction receives a larger penalty than a less confident one.
solutionSteps: The loss is \(-\ln(1-0.9)=-\ln(0.1)=\ln 10\). A confident wrong prediction receives a larger penalty than a less confident one.

ml-logistic-q04.title: Find the weight gradient
ml-logistic-q04.statement: One example has \(x_j=2\), \(y=1\), and current predicted probability \(p=0.75\). Use binary cross-entropy with no penalty.
ml-logistic-q04.prompt: What is \(\partial\ell/\partial w_j\)? Enter a decimal.
ml-logistic-q04.explanation: \((0.75-1)\cdot2=-0.5\). A gradient-descent step increases this weight. With the positive feature, this raises the score and moves the probability toward the true label.
solutionSteps: \((0.75-1)\cdot2=-0.5\). A gradient-descent step increases this weight. With the positive feature, this raises the score and moves the probability toward the true label.

ml-logistic-q05.title: Can more training solve this pattern
ml-logistic-q05.statement: Use \(p=\sigma(w_1x_1+w_2x_2+b)\); predict 1 when \(p\geq0.5\). Positive points: \((1,0),(0,1)\). Negative points: \((0,0),(1,1)\). Only these two raw features are available.
ml-logistic-q05.prompt: Can this model classify all four points correctly?
ml-logistic-q05.hint: Translate the four labels into inequalities on the linear score.
ml-logistic-q05.explanation: The positive points require \(w_1+b\geq0\) and \(w_2+b\geq0\), so \(w_1+w_2+2b\geq0\). The negatives require \(b<0\) and \(w_1+w_2+b<0\), whose sum gives \(w_1+w_2+2b<0\): a contradiction.
solutionSteps: The positive points require \(w_1+b\geq0\) and \(w_2+b\geq0\), so \(w_1+w_2+2b\geq0\). The negatives require \(b<0\) and \(w_1+w_2+b<0\), whose sum gives \(w_1+w_2+2b<0\): a contradiction.

options.a: Yes, by increasing every weight sufficiently.
options.b: Yes, with a sufficiently small learning rate.
options.c: No, these raw features cannot give the required linear boundary.

ml-logistic-q06.title: Does the best finite weight exist
ml-logistic-q06.statement: Model: \(p=\sigma(wx)\), with no bias or penalty. Training examples: \((x,y)=(-1,0),(1,1)\). Minimize mean binary cross-entropy.
ml-logistic-q06.hint: Both examples have the same loss. Examine it as the weight increases.
ml-logistic-q06.explanation: Both losses equal \(\ln(1+e^{-w})\). This is positive and strictly decreasing for every finite \(w\). It tends to 0 as \(w\to+\infty\). The infimum is 0, but no finite weight attains it.
solutionSteps: Both losses equal \(\ln(1+e^{-w})\). This is positive and strictly decreasing for every finite \(w\). It tends to 0 as \(w\to+\infty\). The infimum is 0, but no finite weight attains it.

options.b: The loss approaches zero, but no finite best weight exists.
options.c: A finite positive weight makes the loss exactly zero.

ml-prob-q01.title: Count the false alarms
ml-prob-q01.statement: A batch has 1,000 transactions: 20 fraudulent and 980 legitimate. A detector flags exactly 10% of legitimate transactions.
ml-prob-q01.prompt: How many false positives are there? Enter an integer.
ml-prob-q01.hint: The false-positive rate applies to legitimate transactions.
ml-prob-q01.explanation: There are 0.10 × 980 = 98 false positives. Multiplying by all 1,000 transactions uses the wrong conditioning group.
solutionSteps: There are 0.10 × 980 = 98 false positives. Multiplying by all 1,000 transactions uses the wrong conditioning group.

ml-prob-q02.title: How reliable is a flag
ml-prob-q02.statement: Among flagged transactions, 16 are fraudulent and 98 are legitimate. Select one flagged transaction uniformly at random.
ml-prob-q02.prompt: What is the probability that it is fraudulent?
ml-prob-q02.hint: The denominator is the total number of flags.
ml-prob-q02.explanation: There are \(16+98=114\) flags, so the probability is \(16/114=8/57\), about 14.0%. A detector can find a high fraction of fraud while many of its flags are still false alarms.
solutionSteps: There are \(16+98=114\) flags, so the probability is \(16/114=8/57\), about 14.0%. A detector can find a high fraction of fraud while many of its flags are still false alarms.

ml-prob-q03.title: Combine two independent signals
ml-prob-q03.statement: \(P(Y=1)=P(Y=0)=0.5\). Binary signals A and B are independent given Y. \(P(A=1\mid Y=1)=P(B=1\mid Y=1)=0.8\). Both corresponding probabilities given \(Y=0\) are 0.2.
ml-prob-q03.prompt: When both signals are 1, what is \(P(Y=1\mid A=1,B=1)\)?
ml-prob-q03.hint: Compute a joint likelihood for each class, then normalize.
ml-prob-q03.explanation: The joint likelihoods are \(0.8^2=0.64\) and \(0.2^2=0.04\). Equal priors cancel. The posterior is \(0.64/(0.64+0.04)=16/17\). The value 0.64 alone is an unnormalized likelihood.
solutionSteps: The joint likelihoods are \(0.8^2=0.64\) and \(0.2^2=0.04\). Equal priors cancel. The posterior is \(0.64/(0.64+0.04)=16/17\). The value 0.64 alone is an unnormalized likelihood.

ml-prob-q04.title: Do not count a copied feature twice
ml-prob-q04.statement: \(P(Y=1)=P(Y=0)=0.5\). This time B is an exact copy of A. \(P(A=1\mid Y=1)=0.8\) and \(P(A=1\mid Y=0)=0.2\).
ml-prob-q04.prompt: Given \(A=B=1\), what is the correct posterior probability of class 1? Enter a decimal.
ml-prob-q04.hint: Observing the copy adds no information beyond observing A.
ml-prob-q04.explanation: The event \(A=B=1\) is exactly the event \(A=1\). The posterior is \(0.8/(0.8+0.2)=0.8\). Squaring the likelihoods would wrongly assume conditional independence and produce 16/17.
solutionSteps: The event \(A=B=1\) is exactly the event \(A=1\). The posterior is \(0.8/(0.8+0.2)=0.8\). Squaring the likelihoods would wrongly assume conditional independence and produce 16/17.

ml-prob-q05.title: Fit the class probability
ml-prob-q05.statement: Eight independent Bernoulli observations contain three 1s and five 0s. Fit the shared success probability by maximum likelihood, with no prior or penalty.
ml-prob-q05.prompt: What is the estimate? Enter a decimal.
ml-prob-q05.hint: Count successes and divide by sample size.
ml-prob-q05.explanation: The likelihood is \(\theta^3(1-\theta)^5\). Its log derivative is \(3/\theta-5/(1-\theta)\). Setting it to zero gives \(\theta=3/8=0.375\). The log-likelihood is strictly concave in the interior, and the endpoints have zero likelihood.
solutionSteps: The likelihood is \(\theta^3(1-\theta)^5\). Its log derivative is \(3/\theta-5/(1-\theta)\). Setting it to zero gives \(\theta=3/8=0.375\). The log-likelihood is strictly concave in the interior, and the endpoints have zero likelihood.

ml-prob-q06.title: An event never appeared
ml-prob-q06.statement: Five binary observations contain no successes. Use binary add-one smoothing.
ml-prob-q06.prompt: What estimated probability should be assigned to success?
ml-prob-q06.hint: Add one count to each of the two possible outcomes.
ml-prob-q06.explanation: The estimate is \((0+1)/(5+2)=1/7\). Adding one only to the numerator would fail to account for both outcomes. This estimate is not proof of the true event probability.
solutionSteps: The estimate is \((0+1)/(5+2)=1/7\). Adding one only to the numerator would fail to account for both outcomes. This estimate is not proof of the true event probability.

ml-reg-q01.title: Find the penalized optimum
ml-reg-q01.prompt: Which weight minimizes J? Enter an integer.
ml-reg-q01.hint: Set the derivative of the complete objective to zero.
ml-reg-q01.explanation: \(J'(w)=w-3+2w=3w-3\), so \(w=1\). The second derivative is 3, making this the unique minimum. Minimizing only the data loss would give 3.
solutionSteps: \(J'(w)=w-3+2w=3w-3\), so \(w=1\). The second derivative is 3, making this the unique minimum. Minimizing only the data loss would give 3.

ml-reg-q02.title: Keep the same penalty after rescaling
ml-reg-q02.statement: A scalar model predicts \(wx\) and has penalty \(\lambda w^2/2\), with \(\lambda>0\). Re-express it using \(x'=10x\) and \(w'=w/10\).
ml-reg-q02.prompt: Which \(\lambda'\) preserves the penalty for every w?
ml-reg-q02.hint: Match the coefficient of squared w in the penalty.
ml-reg-q02.explanation: The new penalty is \(\lambda' w^2/200\). Matching \(\lambda w^2/2\) for every w requires \(\lambda'=100\lambda\). Keeping the same coefficient makes the penalty 100 times weaker at corresponding predictions. This concerns the objective, not the learning rate.
solutionSteps: The new penalty is \(\lambda' w^2/200\). Matching \(\lambda w^2/2\) for every w requires \(\lambda'=100\lambda\). Keeping the same coefficient makes the penalty 100 times weaker at corresponding predictions. This concerns the objective, not the learning rate.

ml-reg-q03.title: When does a coefficient become zero
ml-reg-q03.prompt: What is the minimizing weight? Enter a decimal or integer.
ml-reg-q03.hint: Apply soft thresholding with a threshold of 1.
ml-reg-q03.explanation: \(\max(0.6-1,0)=0\), so the minimizer is zero. The objective decreases as we approach zero from the left and increases to the right. Do not differentiate the absolute value at zero as though it were smooth.
solutionSteps: \(\max(0.6-1,0)=0\), so the minimizer is zero. The objective decreases as we approach zero from the left and increases to the right. Do not differentiate the absolute value at zero as though it were smooth.

ml-reg-q04.title: Compare two equivalent representations
ml-reg-q04.statement: Two feature columns are identical. Compare weights A = (2, 0) and B = (1, 1), with the same bias. Use the same data loss and a strictly positive penalty strength \(\lambda\).
ml-reg-q04.prompt: How do L1 and L2 compare these two candidates?
ml-reg-q04.hint: Their predictions agree. Compare absolute sums and sums of squares.
ml-reg-q04.explanation: Both candidates have total weight 2, so identical columns give identical predictions. Their L1 sums both equal 2. The squared sums are 4 for A and 2 for B. L1 ties; L2 strictly prefers B among these two candidates. This does not identify the global best fit.
solutionSteps: Both candidates have total weight 2, so identical columns give identical predictions. Their L1 sums both equal 2. The squared sums are 4 for A and 2 for B. L1 ties; L2 strictly prefers B among these two candidates. This does not identify the global best fit.

options.a: L1 strictly prefers A; L2 strictly prefers B.
options.c: L1 ties; L2 strictly prefers B.

ml-reg-q05.title: Choose the strength, not the training fit
ml-reg-q05.statement: Three converged fits use the same training/validation split and unpenalized predictive loss. \(\lambda=0\): train 0.10, validation 0.25. \(\lambda=1\): train 0.15, validation 0.18. \(\lambda=10\): train 0.25, validation 0.24.
ml-reg-q05.prompt: Select the candidate with the lowest validation loss. Enter its \(\lambda\).
ml-reg-q05.hint: The regularization strength is selected using held-out predictive performance.
ml-reg-q05.explanation: The smallest validation loss is 0.18, achieved at \(\lambda=1\). The lowest training loss does not win this selection rule. The choice is supported by this split; it is not a guarantee about every future sample.
solutionSteps: The smallest validation loss is 0.18, achieved at \(\lambda=1\). The lowest training loss does not win this selection rule. The choice is supported by this split; it is not a guarantee about every future sample.

ml-reg-q06.title: Keep cross-validation honest
ml-reg-q06.statement: You compare regularization strengths by cross-validation on IID rows. Each fit standardizes features using an estimated mean and variance.
ml-reg-q06.prompt: Where should those statistics be fitted in each split?
ml-reg-q06.hint: Keep separate what is fitted from how performance is evaluated.
ml-reg-q06.explanation: Fit the scaler on the training fold and reuse it on the validation fold. Validation may score the candidate, but its values must not fit the scaler. Fitting before the split leaks held-out information; fitting a separate validation scaler changes the transformation.
solutionSteps: Fit the scaler on the training fold and reuse it on the validation fold. Validation may score the candidate, but its values must not fit the scaler. Fitting before the split leaks held-out information; fitting a separate validation scaler changes the transformation.

options.a: On the training fold only; reuse them on the validation fold.
options.b: On training and validation rows together, since labels are unused.
options.c: Separately on training rows and on validation rows.

ml-moments-q01.title: Expected stochastic gradient
ml-moments-q01.statement: At fixed weights, one randomly sampled example has scalar gradient \(G=-2\) with probability 0.25 and \(G=2\) with probability 0.75.
ml-moments-q01.hint: Weight each gradient by its sampling probability.
ml-moments-q01.explanation: \(E[G]=0.25(-2)+0.75(2)=1\). The two possible values are not equally likely, so their unweighted average would be wrong.
solutionSteps: \(E[G]=0.25(-2)+0.75(2)=1\). The two possible values are not equally likely, so their unweighted average would be wrong.

ml-moments-q02.title: Does class balancing preserve the objective
ml-moments-q02.statement: Target: the unweighted mean loss over 10 rows. At fixed weights, the 2 rare-class rows each have scalar gradient 8; the other 8 rows each have gradient -2. A sampler selects each class with probability 0.5, uniformly within class. No importance weights are used.
ml-moments-q02.prompt: Is its sampled gradient unbiased for the target gradient?
ml-moments-q02.hint: Compare the original row-weighted mean with the sampler-weighted mean.
ml-moments-q02.explanation: The target gradient is \((2\cdot8+8\cdot(-2))/10=0\). The sampled gradient has expectation \(0.5(8)+0.5(-2)=3\). Balancing classes changes the objective here; it may be intentional, but it is not an unbiased estimator of the stated target.
solutionSteps: The target gradient is \((2\cdot8+8\cdot(-2))/10=0\). The sampled gradient has expectation \(0.5(8)+0.5(-2)=3\). Balancing classes changes the objective here; it may be intentional, but it is not an unbiased estimator of the stated target.

options.a: Yes; sampling both classes equally always preserves the mean gradient.
options.b: No; its expected gradient is 3, while the target gradient is 0.
options.c: Yes; a larger batch removes the change in expectation.

ml-moments-q03.title: Variance of an independent mini-batch
ml-moments-q03.statement: A mini-batch averages 36 independent draws of a scalar gradient component. Each draw has variance 9; sampling is with replacement at fixed model parameters.
ml-moments-q03.prompt: What is \(\mathrm{Var}(\bar G)\)? Enter a decimal.
ml-moments-q03.hint: The question asks for variance, not standard deviation.
ml-moments-q03.explanation: Independence makes cross-covariances zero. \(\mathrm{Var}(\bar G)=9/36=0.25\). Its standard deviation is 0.5.
solutionSteps: Independence makes cross-covariances zero. \(\mathrm{Var}(\bar G)=9/36=0.25\). Its standard deviation is 0.5.

ml-moments-q04.title: A larger batch with no new information
ml-moments-q04.statement: Draw 18 independent scalar gradients, each with variance 9. Copy each draw exactly once, giving 36 entries. Average all 36 entries.
ml-moments-q04.prompt: What is the variance of this average?
ml-moments-q04.hint: The average of the duplicated entries equals the average of the original draws.
ml-moments-q04.explanation: Writing the original draws as \(G_1,\ldots,G_{18}\), the new mean is \(2\sum_iG_i/36=\sum_iG_i/18\). Its variance is \(9/18=0.5\), not \(9/36\).
solutionSteps: Writing the original draws as \(G_1,\ldots,G_{18}\), the new mean is \(2\sum_iG_i/36=\sum_iG_i/18\). Its variance is \(9/18=0.5\), not \(9/36\).

ml-moments-q05.title: Accuracy standard error
ml-moments-q05.statement: A fixed model has true success probability \(p=0.8\) on each of 400 independent, identically distributed test cases.
ml-moments-q05.prompt: What is the standard error of its test accuracy? Enter probability units, not a percentage.
ml-moments-q05.explanation: \(\sqrt{0.8\cdot0.2/400}=\sqrt{0.0004}=0.02\): two percentage points. If p were unknown, substituting observed accuracy would give a plug-in estimate, not this known-p calculation.
solutionSteps: \(\sqrt{0.8\cdot0.2/400}=\sqrt{0.0004}=0.02\): two percentage points. If p were unknown, substituting observed accuracy would give a plug-in estimate, not this known-p calculation.

ml-moments-q06.title: Equal accuracy is not enough
ml-moments-q06.statement: Two fixed models each score 80% accuracy on the same 400 IID test cases. Only these two aggregate scores are retained.
ml-moments-q06.prompt: Can these scores alone determine the paired standard-error estimate for their accuracy difference?
ml-moments-q06.hint: The two models may agree or fail on different examples.
ml-moments-q06.explanation: No. With identical per-case outcomes, every paired difference is zero. Alternatively, 60% of cases can be correct for both and 20% for each model alone; both still score 80%, but differences vary. The covariance, or equivalent paired disagreement information, is missing.
solutionSteps: No. With identical per-case outcomes, every paired difference is zero. Alternatively, 60% of cases can be correct for both and 20% for each model alone; both still score 80%, but differences vary. The covariance, or equivalent paired disagreement information, is missing.

options.a: Yes; equal accuracies force a standard error of zero.
options.b: Yes; always add two independent accuracy variances.
options.c: No; the paired agreement and disagreement pattern is needed.

ml-generalization-q01.title: Compute expected test error
ml-generalization-q01.statement: At one fixed input, \(f(x)=2\). Across random training sets, the fitted prediction is 1 or 5 with equal probability. Fresh independent label noise has mean 0 and variance 1.
ml-generalization-q01.prompt: What is the expected squared error against a fresh label? Enter a number.
ml-generalization-q01.hint: First find the mean and variance of the fitted prediction.
ml-generalization-q01.explanation: Mean prediction is 3, so squared bias is \((3-2)^2=1\). Prediction variance is \(((1-3)^2+(5-3)^2)/2=4\). Expected test error is \(1+4+1=6\).
solutionSteps: Mean prediction is 3, so squared bias is \((3-2)^2=1\). Prediction variance is \(((1-3)^2+(5-3)^2)/2=4\). Expected test error is \(1+4+1=6\).

ml-generalization-q02.title: Can averaging remove every error
ml-generalization-q02.statement: At one fixed input, independently trained models each have mean prediction 3 and variance 4. The true conditional mean is 2; fresh independent label noise has variance 1. Average M independent model predictions.
ml-generalization-q02.prompt: As M grows without bound, what does expected squared test error approach?
ml-generalization-q02.hint: Averaging reduces variance but does not move the mean prediction to the truth.
ml-generalization-q02.explanation: The average still has mean 3 and squared bias 1. Its variance is \(4/M\). Thus expected error is \(1+4/M+1\), tending to 2. Independence of these model predictions is an explicit assumption.
solutionSteps: The average still has mean 3 and squared bias 1. Its variance is \(4/M\). Thus expected error is \(1+4/M+1\), tending to 2. Independence of these model predictions is an explicit assumption.

ml-generalization-q03.title: Choose the next experiment
ml-generalization-q03.statement: At training sizes 2,000 and 20,000, reliable train/validation losses both plateau near 0.28/0.30. Optimization converged, splits are IID, and a reference model reaches 0.10 using the same available features.
ml-generalization-q03.prompt: Which next experiment is best supported?
ml-generalization-q03.hint: The small gap is not the only evidence: the reference shows room for improvement.
ml-generalization-q03.explanation: Test greater capacity or weaker regularization, and compare held-out loss. The supplied checks make an underfitting investigation reasonable. These curves do not guarantee that the proposed change will succeed.
solutionSteps: Test greater capacity or weaker regularization, and compare held-out loss. The supplied checks make an underfitting investigation reasonable. These curves do not guarantee that the proposed change will succeed.

options.a: Test greater capacity or weaker regularization, then validate.
options.b: Keep the model unchanged and assume more IID data must solve it.
options.c: Treat 0.30 as irreducible noise because the two losses are close.

ml-generalization-q04.title: Training loss rose; is the model worse
ml-generalization-q04.statement: With the same learning procedure and evaluation protocol, increasing IID training data from 500 to 4,000 changes mean train/validation loss from 0.01/0.25 to 0.06/0.13. Repeated-split averages make this change reliable.
ml-generalization-q04.hint: Model selection depends on held-out performance, not just training fit.
ml-generalization-q04.explanation: Held-out loss improved from 0.25 to 0.13 even though fitting the larger training set gave a higher training loss. The gap shrank from 0.24 to 0.07. This supports the benefit of the added data here, without proving a unique cause or unlimited future gains.
solutionSteps: Held-out loss improved from 0.25 to 0.13 even though fitting the larger training set gave a higher training loss. The gap shrank from 0.24 to 0.07. This supports the benefit of the added data here, without proving a unique cause or unlimited future gains.

options.a: The model is worse because training loss increased.
options.b: Held-out performance improved despite a higher training loss.
options.c: The new model has zero bias because its validation loss decreased.

ml-generalization-q05.title: Average correlated predictions
ml-generalization-q05.statement: At a fixed input, four model predictions each have variance 8. Every pair has correlation 0.25. Form their equally weighted average.
ml-generalization-q05.prompt: What is its prediction variance? Enter a decimal.
ml-generalization-q05.explanation: \(\mathrm{Var}(\bar f)=(4\cdot8+2\cdot6\cdot2)/16=56/16=3.5\). There are six distinct pairs. Ignoring their covariance would incorrectly give 2.
solutionSteps: \(\mathrm{Var}(\bar f)=(4\cdot8+2\cdot6\cdot2)/16=56/16=3.5\). There are six distinct pairs. Ignoring their covariance would incorrectly give 2.

ml-generalization-q06.title: Does more randomization guarantee improvement
ml-generalization-q06.statement: A random-forest change considers fewer candidate features per split. Measured pairwise prediction correlation decreases. Bias and individual-tree prediction variance may also change.
ml-generalization-q06.prompt: Does lower correlation alone guarantee lower expected squared test error?
ml-generalization-q06.hint: Separate ensemble variance from total expected error.
ml-generalization-q06.explanation: No. Lower correlation helps the variance formula only with the other quantities controlled. Individual variance can rise and squared bias can increase enough to offset the benefit. Evaluate the complete change on suitable held-out data.
solutionSteps: No. Lower correlation helps the variance formula only with the other quantities controlled. Individual variance can rise and squared bias can increase enough to offset the benefit. Evaluate the complete change on suitable held-out data.

options.a: Yes; any reduction in tree correlation lowers total test error.
options.b: Yes; averaging always removes model bias.
options.c: No; individual variance and bias can offset the correlation benefit.

ml-metrics-q01.title: How many alerts are correct
ml-metrics-q01.statement: A classifier produces TP = 30, FP = 10, FN = 20 and TN = 940 on a held-out set.
ml-metrics-q01.prompt: What is precision for the positive class? Enter a decimal.
ml-metrics-q01.hint: Condition on positive predictions, not actual positives.
ml-metrics-q01.explanation: \(30/(30+10)=0.75\). Recall would be \(30/(30+20)=0.6\); these answer different questions.
solutionSteps: \(30/(30+10)=0.75\). Recall would be \(30/(30+20)=0.6\); these answer different questions.

ml-metrics-q02.title: Combine precision and recall
ml-metrics-q02.statement: On a held-out set, TP = 30, FP = 10, FN = 20 and TN = 940.
ml-metrics-q02.hint: Use the count form rather than the arithmetic mean of precision and recall.
ml-metrics-q02.explanation: \(F_1=60/(60+10+20)=2/3\). The arithmetic mean of precision 0.75 and recall 0.6 is 0.675, which is not F1. TN does not enter this formula.
solutionSteps: \(F_1=60/(60+10+20)=2/3\). The arithmetic mean of precision 0.75 and recall 0.6 is 0.675, which is not F1. TN does not enter this formula.

ml-metrics-q03.title: Choose a cost-sensitive threshold
ml-metrics-q03.statement: Use true deployment posterior probabilities. A false positive costs 2 and a false negative costs 8. Correct decisions cost zero; there are no capacity constraints. Break equal-cost ties toward positive.
ml-metrics-q03.prompt: Predict positive when \(p\geq t\). What is t? Enter a decimal.
ml-metrics-q03.hint: Compare the two conditional expected costs.
ml-metrics-q03.explanation: Choose positive when \(2(1-p)\leq8p\), equivalent to \(p\geq0.2\). This is a cost-minimizing threshold under the stated assumptions, not a universal threshold for every classifier.
solutionSteps: Choose positive when \(2(1-p)\leq8p\), equivalent to \(p\geq0.2\). This is a cost-minimizing threshold under the stated assumptions, not a universal threshold for every classifier.

ml-metrics-q04.title: Lower the threshold
ml-metrics-q04.statement: On the same labeled dataset, keep model scores fixed and lower the positive-prediction threshold. The dataset has positives; both thresholds produce at least one positive prediction.
ml-metrics-q04.hint: The lower threshold only adds predicted positives; those added cases may have either label.
ml-metrics-q04.explanation: True positives cannot decrease, and the number of actual positives is fixed, so recall cannot decrease. Precision can rise or fall depending on the newly included labels. For example, adding only true positives can raise it, while adding only false positives can lower it.
solutionSteps: True positives cannot decrease, and the number of actual positives is fixed, so recall cannot decrease. Precision can rise or fall depending on the newly included labels. For example, adding only true positives can raise it, while adding only false positives can lower it.

options.a: Recall and precision must both increase strictly.
options.b: Recall cannot decrease; precision may increase or decrease.
options.c: ROC-AUC must increase because more positives are predicted.

ml-metrics-q05.title: Same ranking, different probabilities
ml-metrics-q05.statement: Both labels are present in a fixed evaluation set. Transform every score \(s\in[0,1]\) into \(s^2\), using exact arithmetic.
ml-metrics-q05.prompt: What must happen to empirical ROC-AUC?
ml-metrics-q05.hint: Squaring is strictly increasing on [0,1], including preservation of ties.
ml-metrics-q05.explanation: All positive-negative orderings and ties are preserved, so ROC-AUC is unchanged. Calibration need not survive, and predictions at a fixed numerical threshold can change. The result does not require the original scores to be calibrated.
solutionSteps: All positive-negative orderings and ties are preserved, so ROC-AUC is unchanged. Calibration need not survive, and predictions at a fixed numerical threshold can change. The result does not require the original scores to be calibrated.

options.b: It decreases because every score becomes smaller or equal.
options.c: It increases because squaring makes predictions more confident.

ml-metrics-q06.title: Evaluate generalization to new users
ml-metrics-q06.statement: A dataset has many rows per user. The deployment target is entirely unseen users from the same user population. No future-time extrapolation is being claimed.
ml-metrics-q06.prompt: Which split best matches that target?
ml-metrics-q06.hint: Prevent a user identity from appearing in more than one split.
ml-metrics-q06.explanation: Use user-disjoint training, validation and test sets. Random row splits can place the same user in both training and evaluation, answering an easier seen-user question. Fit preprocessing on training data; use validation for selection and keep the final test untouched.
solutionSteps: Use user-disjoint training, validation and test sets. Random row splits can place the same user in both training and evaluation, answering an easier seen-user question. Fit preprocessing on training data; use validation for selection and keep the final test untouched.

options.a: Randomly split rows, allowing each user in all sets.
options.b: Group rows by user, but choose the best model repeatedly on the test set.
options.c: Split by user into disjoint train, validation and test groups.

ml-nn-weight-shape.title: Choose the weight shape
ml-nn-weight-shape.statement: Use \(Z=XW+b\). A batch X has shape \(8\times6\). The layer must output 4 features per example.
ml-nn-weight-shape.hint: The inner dimensions must match; each input row becomes one output row.
ml-nn-weight-shape.explanation: \((8\times6)(6\times4)\) produces \(8\times4\). This convention defines W directly; a library may store its transpose.
solutionSteps: \((8\times6)(6\times4)\) produces \(8\times4\). This convention defines W directly; a library may store its transpose.

ml-nn-parameter-count.title: Count the trainable parameters
ml-nn-parameter-count.statement: A fully connected network has 6 input features, 4 hidden units, and 3 outputs. Each layer has one bias per output unit. Activations add no parameters.
ml-nn-parameter-count.prompt: How many trainable scalar parameters are there?
ml-nn-parameter-count.hint: Count weights and biases separately for each of the two layers.
ml-nn-parameter-count.explanation: The first layer has \(6\cdot4+4=28\) parameters; the second has \(4\cdot3+3=15\). Total: 43.
solutionSteps: The first layer has \(6\cdot4+4=28\) parameters; the second has \(4\cdot3+3=15\). Total: 43.

ml-nn-active-gradient.title: Follow the active path
ml-nn-active-gradient.hint: Compute the prediction first, then multiply the error by v and x.
ml-nn-active-gradient.explanation: \(z=1\) and \(\hat y=3\). Thus \((3-1)\cdot3\cdot2=12\). Forgetting the output weight v would give the wrong gradient.
solutionSteps: \(z=1\) and \(\hat y=3\). Thus \((3-1)\cdot3\cdot2=12\). Forgetting the output weight v would give the wrong gradient.

ml-nn-inactive-gradient.title: A mistake with no incoming gradient
ml-nn-inactive-gradient.hint: Check whether the preactivation is positive before using the active-path formula.
ml-nn-inactive-gradient.explanation: \(z=-1\), so \(\hat y=0\) and \(L=1/2\). ReLU is locally flat: the gradient is 0 despite the positive loss.
solutionSteps: \(z=-1\), so \(\hat y=0\) and \(L=1/2\). ReLU is locally flat: the gradient is 0 despite the positive loss.

ml-nn-stable-softmax.title: Avoid exponential overflow
ml-nn-stable-softmax.statement: A classifier produces logits \((1000,1001,999)\). You will evaluate softmax.
ml-nn-stable-softmax.prompt: Which replacement subtracts the maximum and preserves the probabilities?
ml-nn-stable-softmax.hint: Subtract 1001 from each entry, keeping the order.
ml-nn-stable-softmax.explanation: The replacement is \((-1,0,-2)\). A common shift cancels between numerator and denominator in exact arithmetic; all resulting exponentials are at most 1.
solutionSteps: The replacement is \((-1,0,-2)\). A common shift cancels between numerator and denominator in exact arithmetic; all resulting exponentials are at most 1.

ml-nn-cross-entropy-gradient.title: Differentiate the correct-class logit
ml-nn-cross-entropy-gradient.statement: Softmax probabilities are \((0.2,0.5,0.3)\). The true class is the second class. Use one-example, unweighted cross-entropy with no label smoothing.
ml-nn-cross-entropy-gradient.prompt: What is \(\partial L/\partial z_2\)? Enter a decimal.
ml-nn-cross-entropy-gradient.hint: Subtract the second target entry from the second probability.
ml-nn-cross-entropy-gradient.explanation: \(p_2-y_2=0.5-1=-0.5\). Gradient descent increases this logit when other logits are treated as fixed.
solutionSteps: \(p_2-y_2=0.5-1=-0.5\). Gradient descent increases this logit when other logits are treated as fixed.

ml-attention-output-shape.title: Track the output shape
ml-attention-output-shape.statement: For one head, Q and K both have shape \(4\times3\); V has shape \(4\times2\). Compute \(\mathrm{softmax}(QK^T/\sqrt{3})V\). No output projection.
ml-attention-output-shape.hint: First find the score-matrix shape; then multiply the attention weights by V.
ml-attention-output-shape.explanation: The score matrix is \(4\times4\). Multiplying it by \(4\times2\) gives \(4\times2\): one value-sized output per query.
solutionSteps: The score matrix is \(4\times4\). Multiplying it by \(4\times2\) gives \(4\times2\): one value-sized output per query.

ml-attention-weighted-value.title: Calculate one attention output
ml-attention-weighted-value.statement: One query has already-scaled logits \((0,\ln3)\) and scalar values \((2,6)\). Neither key is masked. No dropout.
ml-attention-weighted-value.prompt: What scalar output does attention produce?
ml-attention-weighted-value.hint: Exponentiate the two logits, normalize, and combine the values.
ml-attention-weighted-value.explanation: Exponentials are \((1,3)\), so weights are \((1/4,3/4)\). The output is \(2/4+18/4=5\).
solutionSteps: Exponentials are \((1,3)\), so weights are \((1/4,3/4)\). The output is \(2/4+18/4=5\).

ml-attention-scaled-variance.title: Check the attention scale
ml-attention-scaled-variance.statement: Vectors q and k have 64 coordinates each. All 128 coordinates are mutually independent with mean 0 and variance 1.
ml-attention-scaled-variance.hint: Variance scales by the square of the multiplier.
ml-attention-scaled-variance.explanation: Each product has variance 1, and the 64 products are independent. The sum has variance 64. Dividing by 8 gives variance \(64/8^2=1\).
solutionSteps: Each product has variance 1, and the 64 products are independent. The sum has variance 64. Dividing by 8 gives variance \(64/8^2=1\).

ml-attention-causal-output.title: Remove the future token
ml-attention-causal-output.statement: At query position 2 of 3, already-scaled logits are \((\ln2,0,\ln5)\) and scalar values are \((3,9,100)\). A causal mask allows positions 1 and 2 only. No dropout.
ml-attention-causal-output.prompt: What scalar attention output is correct?
ml-attention-causal-output.hint: Remove the third score before computing the softmax denominator.
ml-attention-causal-output.explanation: Allowed exponentials are 2 and 1, so weights are \((2/3,1/3,0)\). The output is \(2+3=5\). Unmasked attention gives 64.375; zeroing the future weight afterward without renormalizing gives 1.875.
solutionSteps: Allowed exponentials are 2 and 1, so weights are \((2/3,1/3,0)\). The output is \(2+3=5\). Unmasked attention gives 64.375; zeroing the future weight afterward without renormalizing gives 1.875.

ml-attention-score-memory.title: Extend the context
ml-attention-score-memory.statement: An implementation explicitly stores the complete dense self-attention score tensor. Increase sequence length from 1,024 to 2,048; batch size, head count and data type stay fixed.
ml-attention-score-memory.prompt: By what factor does this tensor grow?
ml-attention-score-memory.hint: Both the query and key dimensions double.
ml-attention-score-memory.explanation: \((2048/1024)^2=4\). This is the score tensor, not a claim that all model memory grows by four.
solutionSteps: \((2048/1024)^2=4\). This is the score tensor, not a claim that all model memory grows by four.

ml-attention-kv-cache.title: Budget one layer of KV cache
ml-attention-kv-cache.statement: One layer caches 1,024 tokens for one sequence. It has 8 key/value heads with 64 entries per key and per value; each entry uses 2 bytes. Count K and V only, with no extra capacity or overhead.
ml-attention-kv-cache.prompt: How many MiB are stored? Use \(1\ \mathrm{MiB}=2^{20}\) bytes.
ml-attention-kv-cache.hint: Multiply tokens, heads, entries, and bytes; include both K and V.
ml-attention-kv-cache.explanation: \(2\cdot1\cdot1024\cdot8\cdot64\cdot2=2{,}097{,}152\) bytes, or 2 MiB. Model weights and temporary activations are excluded.
solutionSteps: \(2\cdot1\cdot1024\cdot8\cdot64\cdot2=2{,}097{,}152\) bytes, or 2 MiB. Model weights and temporary activations are excluded.

ml-serving-throughput.title: Calculate ideal throughput
ml-serving-throughput.statement: A worker processes full batches of 32 requests in 40 ms each, serially. Each request contains one example. Assume constant backlog, no overhead, and no overlap.
ml-serving-throughput.prompt: What is its ideal throughput in requests per second?
ml-serving-throughput.hint: Convert milliseconds to seconds before dividing.
ml-serving-throughput.explanation: \(32/0.040=800\) requests/s. This is an ideal service rate, not a sustainable arrival-rate guarantee with a latency target.
solutionSteps: \(32/0.040=800\) requests/s. This is an ideal service rate, not a sustainable arrival-rate guarantee with a latency target.

ml-serving-tail-latency.title: Can the mean certify the target?
ml-serving-tail-latency.statement: At the intended load, a service has mean end-to-end latency 20 ms. The target is p99 at most 100 ms.
ml-serving-tail-latency.prompt: Does the mean establish that the target is met?
ml-serving-tail-latency.hint: A small fraction of very slow requests can coexist with a low mean.
ml-serving-tail-latency.explanation: No. For example, 98% of requests at 10 ms and 2% at 510 ms have mean 20 ms but p99 510 ms. Constant 20 ms latency has the same mean and a different p99.
solutionSteps: No. For example, 98% of requests at 10 ms and 2% at 510 ms have mean 20 ms but p99 510 ms. Constant 20 ms latency has the same mean and a different p99.

options.c: No; the latency distribution or p99 measurement is needed.

ml-experiment-relative-uplift.title: Report the relative improvement
ml-experiment-relative-uplift.statement: In a randomized test, 100 of 1,000 control users convert and 120 of 1,000 treatment users convert. Each user contributes one binary outcome.
ml-experiment-relative-uplift.prompt: What is the observed relative uplift, as a percentage? Enter 20 for 20%.
ml-experiment-relative-uplift.hint: Divide the difference in rates by the control rate.
ml-experiment-relative-uplift.explanation: \((0.12-0.10)/0.10=0.20\), or 20%. The absolute change is 0.02, or 2 percentage points. This point estimate alone does not establish significance.
solutionSteps: \((0.12-0.10)/0.10=0.20\), or 20%. The absolute change is 0.02, or 2 percentage points. This point estimate alone does not establish significance.

ml-experiment-interval.title: Interpret an inconclusive interval
ml-experiment-interval.statement: A planned fixed-horizon test reports a valid 95% confidence interval of [-1, 5] percentage points for treatment minus control conversion. The analysis uses one prespecified metric.
ml-experiment-interval.hint: The interval includes negative, zero, and positive effects.
ml-experiment-interval.explanation: The interval does not establish a positive effect and does not prove zero effect. It is not a 95% posterior probability that this particular true effect lies in the reported interval.
solutionSteps: The interval does not establish a positive effect and does not prove zero effect. It is not a 95% posterior probability that this particular true effect lies in the reported interval.

options.a: The result does not establish a positive effect or prove no effect.
options.b: The treatment has no effect because zero is included.
options.c: The treatment is beneficial because the upper bound is positive.

ml-experiment-analysis-unit.title: Use the right analysis unit
ml-experiment-analysis-unit.statement: An experiment randomizes independent users, each with many correlated sessions. The target is mean total clicks per user during a fixed window. Assume no spillovers between users.
ml-experiment-analysis-unit.hint: Keep the randomized user as the unit and include users with zero clicks.
ml-experiment-analysis-unit.explanation: Compute total clicks for every assigned user, including zeros, and compare user-level means with user-level uncertainty. Treating sessions as independent both ignores within-user dependence and changes the weighting.
solutionSteps: Compute total clicks for every assigned user, including zeros, and compare user-level means with user-level uncertainty. Treating sessions as independent both ignores within-user dependence and changes the weighting.

options.a: Treat every session as an independent sample.
options.b: Aggregate clicks per assigned user and analyze those user totals.
options.c: Keep only users who clicked at least once.

ml-experiment-optional-stopping.title: Avoid a false-positive shortcut
ml-experiment-optional-stopping.statement: A team uses an ordinary fixed-horizon test at the 5% significance level. It checks hourly and stops as soon as a positive result has p < 0.05, without a sequential correction.
ml-experiment-optional-stopping.prompt: Is the usual 5% false-positive guarantee preserved?
ml-experiment-optional-stopping.hint: The stopping rule is now chosen using the observed results.
ml-experiment-optional-stopping.explanation: No. Repeated success-based stopping can increase the false-positive probability. Prespecifying that rule alone is insufficient: use a valid sequential method or the planned fixed-horizon analysis. The exact inflation depends on the testing process.
solutionSteps: No. Repeated success-based stopping can increase the false-positive probability. Prespecifying that rule alone is insufficient: use a valid sequential method or the planned fixed-horizon analysis. The exact inflation depends on the testing process.

options.a: Yes, because every individual check uses 0.05.
options.b: Yes, if the hourly schedule was announced in advance.
options.c: No; this stopping rule requires an appropriate sequential procedure.

cs-u10-q01.title: Count three transitions
cs-u10-q01.statement: Three services a, b and c have directed edges in both directions between every distinct pair, and no loops. A is their adjacency matrix.
cs-u10-q01.hint: List all three-edge walks starting at a and ending at b; intermediate vertices may repeat.
cs-u10-q01.explanation: The walks are abab, abcb and acab. Each follows three edges, and there are no others. The count is 3.
solutionSteps: The walks are abab, abcb and acab. Each follows three edges, and there are no others. The count is 3.

cs-u10-q02.title: Debug a path-counting claim
cs-u10-q02.statement: A loop-free directed graph has only three vertices a, b and c. Both directions exist between every distinct pair. Its adjacency matrix satisfies \((A^3)_{ab}=3\).
cs-u10-q02.prompt: A programmer reports three paths of length 3 from a to b. What is wrong?
cs-u10-q02.hint: A length-3 path would need four distinct vertices.
cs-u10-q02.explanation: The matrix entry counts three walks. A path of length 3 requires four distinct vertices, but this graph has only three. Thus there are no length-3 paths.
solutionSteps: The matrix entry counts three walks. A path of length 3 requires four distinct vertices, but this graph has only three. Thus there are no length-3 paths.

options.a: The matrix must be multiplied using Boolean arithmetic to count walks.
options.b: Those are walks with repetitions; none is a length-3 path.
options.c: The entry counts paths from b to a instead.

cs-u10-q03.title: Find the minimum number of slots
cs-u10-q03.statement: Tasks A-F each take one slot. Prerequisites: \(A\to C\), \(B\to C\), \(B\to D\), \(C\to E\), \(D\to E\), \(E\to F\). Processors are unlimited; a task starts only after all prerequisites finish.
cs-u10-q03.prompt: What is the minimum number of slots?
cs-u10-q03.hint: Give both a chain that forces the lower bound and a schedule attaining it.
cs-u10-q03.explanation: The chain \(A\to C\to E\to F\) forces four slots. The schedule {A,B}, {C,D}, {E}, {F} meets every dependency and uses four slots.
solutionSteps: The chain \(A\to C\to E\to F\) forces four slots. The schedule {A,B}, {C,D}, {E}, {F} meets every dependency and uses four slots.

cs-u10-q04.title: Look beyond direct dependencies
cs-u10-q04.statement: Tasks A-F each take one slot, with unlimited processors. Edges: \(A\to B\), \(A\to C\), \(B\to D\), \(C\to E\), \(D\to F\), \(E\to F\).
cs-u10-q04.prompt: Which pair can occupy the same slot in some valid schedule?
cs-u10-q04.hint: Check for a directed path in either direction, not just a direct edge.
cs-u10-q04.explanation: B and E are incomparable. A valid schedule is {A}, {C}, {B,E}, {D}, {F}. In contrast, \(A\to C\to E\) and \(C\to E\to F\) forbid the other two pairs.
solutionSteps: B and E are incomparable. A valid schedule is {A}, {C}, {B,E}, {D}, {F}. In contrast, \(A\to C\to E\) and \(C\to E\to F\) forbid the other two pairs.

cs-u10-q05.title: Count the mutual-reachability classes
cs-u10-q05.statement: The vertices are A-F. The only edges are \(A\to B\), \(B\to C\), \(C\to A\), \(C\to D\), \(D\to E\), \(E\to D\), \(E\to F\).
cs-u10-q05.prompt: How many strongly connected components are there?
cs-u10-q05.hint: Group vertices that can reach each other in both directions; singletons count.
cs-u10-q05.explanation: The classes are {A,B,C}, {D,E}, and {F}. Edges between these groups go only forward, so no two groups can merge into one mutual-reachability class.
solutionSteps: The classes are {A,B,C}, {D,E}, and {F}. Edges between these groups go only forward, so no two groups can merge into one mutual-reachability class.

cs-u10-q06.title: Find the failed order axiom
cs-u10-q06.statement: A graph has edges \(a\to b\), \(b\to a\), and \(b\to c\). Define uRv to mean v is reachable from u, including zero-length walks.
cs-u10-q06.prompt: Which requirement prevents R from being a nonstrict partial order?
cs-u10-q06.hint: Test the two distinct vertices that reach each other.
cs-u10-q06.explanation: Reachability is reflexive because zero-length walks are allowed, and transitive by concatenation. Antisymmetry fails: aRb and bRa hold although a and b are distinct.
solutionSteps: Reachability is reflexive because zero-length walks are allowed, and transitive by concatenation. Antisymmetry fails: aRb and bRa hold although a and b are distinct.

cs-u11-q01.title: Count the busiest switch
cs-u11-q01.statement: Four packets have distinct input and output terminals. Their switch sequences are (a,x,d), (b,x,e), (c,y,f), and (g,x,h). All listed switches are distinct except the repeated x.
cs-u11-q01.hint: Count how many paths contain each switch.
cs-u11-q01.explanation: Switch x lies on three packet paths. Every other switch lies on one. The maximum switch load is therefore 3; path length is a different measure.
solutionSteps: Switch x lies on three packet paths. Every other switch lies on one. The maximum switch load is therefore 3; path length is a different measure.

cs-u11-q02.title: Do detours redefine diameter?
cs-u11-q02.statement: A network has a shortest path of at most 4 edges for every input-output pair. One chosen permutation routing deliberately uses a 7-edge path.
cs-u11-q02.prompt: What follows about its input-output diameter?
cs-u11-q02.hint: Diameter uses shortest paths, even when the actual routing selects another path.
cs-u11-q02.explanation: The diameter is at most 4. The selected routing has latency at least 7, but that detour does not change any shortest-path distance.
solutionSteps: The diameter is at most 4. The selected routing has latency at least 7, but that detour does not change any shortest-path distance.

options.a: The diameter must be at least 7.
options.c: The diameter equals the routing congestion.

cs-u11-q03.title: Meet a switch budget and a hop limit
cs-u11-q03.statement: Choose one of the book's binary-tree, grid or butterfly designs for N = 16. The budget is at most 100 switches and the input-output diameter must be at most 8 edges, including terminal links.
cs-u11-q03.hint: Use \(\log_2 16=4\) and check both columns for every design.
cs-u11-q03.explanation: Tree: 31 switches, diameter 10. Grid: 256 switches, diameter 32. Butterfly: 80 switches, diameter 6. Only the butterfly satisfies both limits.
solutionSteps: Tree: 31 switches, diameter 10. Grid: 256 switches, diameter 32. Butterfly: 80 switches, diameter 6. Only the butterfly satisfies both limits.

cs-u11-q04.title: A shallow tree can still bottleneck
cs-u11-q04.statement: In the book's N = 16 binary-tree network, a permutation sends every input in the left half to an output in the right half, and every right-half input to a left-half output. Routes through the tree are unique.
cs-u11-q04.prompt: How many packet paths must pass through the root switch?
cs-u11-q04.hint: Removing the root separates the two halves; count traffic in both directions.
cs-u11-q04.explanation: All 16 packets cross between halves. Every route therefore uses the root, giving it load 16. Counting only left-to-right packets would miss half the traffic.
solutionSteps: All 16 packets cross between halves. Every route therefore uses the root, giving it load 16. Counting only left-to-right packets would miss half the traffic.

cs-u11-q05.title: Propagate the routing constraints
cs-u11-q05.statement: Packets a-f must be split between Upper and Lower. Input-conflict pairs: (a,b), (c,d), (e,f). Output-conflict pairs: (b,c), (d,e), (f,a). Each pair must be split. Packet a takes Upper.
cs-u11-q05.prompt: Which other packets must take Upper?
cs-u11-q05.explanation: The constraints force b to Lower, c to Upper, d to Lower, e to Upper and f to Lower. The last pair (f,a) is consistent. Thus c and e join a.
solutionSteps: The constraints force b to Lower, c to Upper, d to Lower, e to Upper and f to Lower. The last pair (f,a) is consistent. Thus c and e join a.

cs-u11-q06.title: Read the guarantee precisely
cs-u11-q06.statement: A Beneš network has congestion 1 in the book's sense. A programmer lets each packet independently choose any path to its assigned output.
cs-u11-q06.prompt: Does the theorem guarantee congestion 1 for those choices?
cs-u11-q06.hint: Distinguish existence of a good routing from every routing being good.
cs-u11-q06.explanation: No. For each permutation, a coordinated choice of paths with congestion 1 exists. Arbitrary independent paths may share switches. The theorem does not turn every choice into an optimal routing.
solutionSteps: No. For each permutation, a coordinated choice of paths with congestion 1 exists. Arbitrary independent paths may share switches. The theorem does not turn every choice into an optimal routing.

options.a: Yes; every path selection has congestion 1.
options.b: No; the paths may need to be coordinated.
options.c: No; some permutations have no congestion-1 routing.

cs-u12-q01.title: Reject an inconsistent degree report
cs-u12-q01.statement: A report describes a simple undirected graph with 8 vertices. Seven vertices have degree 3; the remaining vertex has degree 4.
cs-u12-q01.prompt: Can this degree report be correct?
cs-u12-q01.hint: Add the degrees before trying to draw the graph.
cs-u12-q01.explanation: The sum is \(7\cdot3+4=25\), which is odd. It cannot equal twice an integer number of edges. Hence no such graph exists.

cs-u14-q01.title: Count a triangular loop
cs-u14-q01.statement: For every integer \(i=1,\ldots,n\), a loop processes \(j=1,\ldots,i-1\). Each pair (i,j) performs one comparison; \(n\ge1\). An empty inner range performs none.

solutionSteps: The count is \(\sum_{i=1}^{n}(i-1)=\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}j=n(n-1)/2\). In particular, n = 1 gives zero comparisons. Counting n comparisons for every outer iteration ignores the changing bound.

cs-u14-q02.title: Total the copies during growth

cs-u14-q02.hint: Each resize copies the old capacity, including 256 on the final resize.
cs-u14-q02.explanation: The copied counts are \(1,2,4,\ldots,256\), so the total is \(\sum_{i=0}^{8}2^i=2^9-1=511\). The new capacity 512 is not itself copied during that final resize.
solutionSteps: The copied counts are \(1,2,4,\ldots,256\), so the total is \(\sum_{i=0}^{8}2^i=2^9-1=511\). The new capacity 512 is not itself copied during that final resize.

cs-u14-q03.title: Keep the approximation error
cs-u14-q03.statement: A cost model is \(R(n)=n\sum_{i=1}^{n}1/i=nH_n\) for integers \(n\ge2\). Use the stated harmonic bounds; ln denotes the natural logarithm.
cs-u14-q03.hint: Multiply both sides of each harmonic bound by n, including the endpoint correction.
cs-u14-q03.explanation: Multiplying by n gives \(n\ln n+1\le R(n)\le n\ln n+n\). The upper error term grows with n, so replacing it by 1 or treating the logarithmic expression as exact is unjustified.
solutionSteps: Multiplying by n gives \(n\ln n+1\le R(n)\le n\ln n+n\). The upper error term grows with n, so replacing it by 1 or treating the logarithmic expression as exact is unjustified.

cs-u14-q04.title: Analyze a loop with integer division
cs-u14-q04.statement: For \(i=1,\ldots,n\), a loop performs exactly \(\lfloor n/i\rfloor\) operations. Thus \(T(n)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\lfloor n/i\rfloor\). Consider positive integer n growing without bound.
cs-u14-q04.prompt: Which is the tight asymptotic order?
cs-u14-q04.hint: Compare T(n) with \(nH_n\). The sum of all rounding losses is less than n.
cs-u14-q04.explanation: The floor bounds give \(nH_n-n<T(n)\le nH_n\). Using the harmonic bounds gives \(n\ln n-n+1<T(n)\le n\ln n+n\). For sufficiently large n, both sides are positive constant multiples of \(n\ln n\). Therefore \(T(n)=\Theta(n\log n)\) for any fixed logarithm base greater than 1.
solutionSteps: The floor bounds give \(nH_n-n<T(n)\le nH_n\). Using the harmonic bounds gives \(n\ln n-n+1<T(n)\le n\ln n+n\). For sufficiently large n, both sides are positive constant multiples of \(n\ln n\). Therefore \(T(n)=\Theta(n\log n)\) for any fixed logarithm base greater than 1.

cs-u14-q05.explanation: \(3^{n+2}/3^n=9\), a fixed constant. The other ratios are n and \(3^n\), both unbounded. Only the constant shift in the exponent preserves this O-bound.
solutionSteps: \(3^{n+2}/3^n=9\), a fixed constant. The other ratios are n and \(3^n\), both unbounded. Only the constant shift in the exponent preserves this O-bound.

cs-u14-q06.explanation: For every n, \(n\le T(n)\le3n\), proving \(T(n)=\Theta(n)\). However, \(T(n)/n\) alternates between 1 and 3 and has no limit. In particular, it does not tend to 1.
solutionSteps: For every n, \(n\le T(n)\le3n\), proving \(T(n)=\Theta(n)\). However, \(T(n)/n\) alternates between 1 and 3 and has no limit. In particular, it does not tend to 1.

cs-u16-q01.title: Encode two independent capacity choices
cs-u16-q01.statement: A configuration is determined by a pair of counts (a,b). The allowed A count is 0, 1 or 2; the allowed B count is any nonnegative even integer. Total size is a+b. Each permitted pair counts once, and order is irrelevant.

cs-u16-q01.hint: Write one series for each allowed count, then multiply them.
cs-u16-q01.explanation: A contributes \(1+x+x^2\) and B contributes \(1+x^2+x^4+\cdots=1/(1-x^2)\). Therefore the product is \((1+x+x^2)/(1-x^2)\). Squaring \(1+x\) would count two different ways to obtain A count 1.
solutionSteps: A contributes \(1+x+x^2\) and B contributes \(1+x^2+x^4+\cdots=1/(1-x^2)\). Therefore the product is \((1+x+x^2)/(1-x^2)\). Squaring \(1+x\) would count two different ways to obtain A count 1.

cs-u16-q02.explanation: The size pairs (0,4) and (2,2) contribute \(1\cdot1\) and \(2\cdot2\). The pair (1,3) contributes zero because B has no size-3 term. The total is \(1+4=5\), not the product of the two size-4 coefficients.

cs-u16-q05.title: Find the missing initial-condition correction
cs-u16-q05.statement: A sequence satisfies \(a_0=2\), \(a_1=5\), and \(a_n=3a_{n-1}-2a_{n-2}\) for \(n\ge2\). Let \(F(x)=\sum_{n\ge0}a_nx^n\).

cs-u17-q02.explanation: The empty set has probability \(1/3\), while the singleton \(\{a\}\) has probability \((1/3)(1/2)=1/6\). Similarly, \(\{b\}\) has probability \(1/6\) and \(\{a,b\}\) has probability \(1/3\). Uniform choice at each stage does not make all four outputs equally likely.
solutionSteps: The empty set has probability \(1/3\), while the singleton \(\{a\}\) has probability \((1/3)(1/2)=1/6\). Similarly, \(\{b\}\) has probability \(1/6\) and \(\{a,b\}\) has probability \(1/3\). Uniform choice at each stage does not make all four outputs equally likely.

cs-u17-q04.statement: Four checks each fail with probability 0.02 on a randomly selected run. Their dependence is unknown.
cs-u17-q04.prompt: What is the smallest universal upper bound on at least one failure from this information?
cs-u17-q04.hint: Add the four probabilities. Could four disjoint failure events attain that sum?
cs-u17-q04.explanation: The union bound gives \(P(\text{at least one})\le4(0.02)=0.08\). Equality is possible if the four failure events are disjoint, so no smaller universal upper bound follows. The product formula would require independence.

cs-u17-q05.title: Find the exact collision probability
cs-u17-q05.statement: Four distinct keys hash independently and uniformly into eight buckets. A collision means that some two keys land in the same bucket.
cs-u17-q05.prompt: What is the probability of at least one collision?
cs-u17-q05.hint: Compute the probability that all four buckets chosen are distinct, then take its complement.
cs-u17-q05.explanation: The no-collision probability is \((8\cdot7\cdot6\cdot5)/8^4=105/256\). The complement is \(151/256\). The value \(6/8\) is a union bound, not the exact probability.
solutionSteps: The no-collision probability is \((8\cdot7\cdot6\cdot5)/8^4=105/256\). The complement is \(151/256\). The value \(6/8\) is a union bound, not the exact probability.

cs-u17-q06.title: Choose enough hash bits for a bound
cs-u17-q06.statement: Sixteen distinct keys hash independently and uniformly into \(2^b\) buckets, where b is a positive integer. Use the pairwise union bound to certify collision probability at most \(1/32\).
cs-u17-q06.prompt: What is the smallest b certified by this bound?
cs-u17-q06.explanation: The bound requires \(2^b\ge3840\). Since \(2^{11}=2048<3840\le4096=2^{12}\), b = 12 is the smallest certified value. This answers the stated bound-based design question, not a claim about arbitrary hash functions.

cs-u18-q01.title: Both failed, given at least one failed
cs-u18-q01.statement: Two attempts fail independently, each with probability \(1/4\). You learn that at least one failed; no particular attempt is identified.
cs-u18-q01.prompt: What is the probability that both failed?
cs-u18-q01.hint: The conditioning event excludes only the outcome in which both succeed.
cs-u18-q01.explanation: \(P(\text{both fail})=1/16\), while \(P(\text{at least one fails})=1-(3/4)^2=7/16\). Their ratio is \(1/7\). Conditioning on a named attempt failing would be different information.
solutionSteps: \(P(\text{both fail})=1/16\), while \(P(\text{at least one fails})=1-(3/4)^2=7/16\). Their ratio is \(1/7\). Conditioning on a named attempt failing would be different information.

cs-u18-q02.title: Which deployment produced the failure?
cs-u18-q02.statement: A handles 20% of requests and B handles 80%. Failure probabilities are 0.04 on A and 0.01 on B. Select a request at random and observe that it failed.
cs-u18-q02.prompt: What is the probability that it came from A? Enter a decimal.
cs-u18-q02.hint: Weight each deployment failure rate by its share of traffic, then normalize.
cs-u18-q02.explanation: A contributes \(0.2(0.04)=0.008\) to the failure probability; B contributes \(0.8(0.01)=0.008\). Thus \(P(A\mid\text{failure})=0.008/0.016=0.5\). The 0.04 rate conditions in the opposite direction.
solutionSteps: A contributes \(0.2(0.04)=0.008\) to the failure probability; B contributes \(0.8(0.01)=0.008\). Thus \(P(A\mid\text{failure})=0.008/0.016=0.5\). The 0.04 rate conditions in the opposite direction.

cs-u18-q03.title: Weight the actual traffic mix
cs-u18-q03.statement: 90% of requests are small and fail with probability 0.01. The remaining 10% are large and fail with probability 0.20.
cs-u18-q03.prompt: What is the overall failure probability? Enter a decimal.
cs-u18-q03.hint: Use the traffic share as the weight for each conditional rate.
cs-u18-q03.explanation: \(0.9(0.01)+0.1(0.20)=0.029\). The unweighted average 0.105 would describe a 50/50 traffic mixture, not the stated one.
solutionSteps: \(0.9(0.01)+0.1(0.20)=0.029\). The unweighted average 0.105 would describe a 50/50 traffic mixture, not the stated one.

cs-u18-q04.statement: Observed successes: A has 9/10 on easy tasks and 4/10 on hard tasks. B has 80/100 on easy tasks and 1/5 on hard tasks. Each fraction is successes divided by tasks.

With the same easy/hard weights, A would have the higher weighted rate because both its group rates are higher. The observed aggregates alone do not establish which system causes better outcomes.

cs-u18-q05.title: Can two exclusive error codes be independent?
cs-u18-q05.statement: A request returns exactly one status code. Let A mean code 400 and B mean code 500, with probabilities 0.2 and 0.3 respectively.
cs-u18-q05.hint: A request cannot return both of these mutually exclusive codes.
cs-u18-q05.explanation: \(P(A\cap B)=0\), whereas \(P(A)P(B)=0.06\). The events are disjoint but not independent: observing either rules out the other.
solutionSteps: \(P(A\cap B)=0\), whereas \(P(A)P(B)=0.06\). The events are disjoint but not independent: observing either rules out the other.

options.b: Yes: distinct status codes cannot influence each other.

cs-u18-q06.title: Pairwise checks miss a parity constraint
cs-u18-q06.statement: A generator chooses uniformly from \(000,011,101,110\). Let \(A_i\) be the event that bit i is 1, for \(i=1,2,3\).
cs-u18-q06.hint: Count the probability of a 1 in any position, two specified 1s, and three 1s.
cs-u18-q06.explanation: Each event has probability \(1/2\) and each pair intersection has probability \(1/4\), so all pairs are independent. But \(P(A_1\cap A_2\cap A_3)=0\ne(1/2)^3\). Thus the family is not mutually independent.
solutionSteps: Each event has probability \(1/2\) and each pair intersection has probability \(1/4\), so all pairs are independent. But \(P(A_1\cap A_2\cap A_3)=0\ne(1/2)^3\). Thus the family is not mutually independent.

options.b: No pair of these events is independent.
options.c: They are pairwise independent but not mutually independent.

cs-u19-q01.title: Count exactly one failure
cs-u19-q01.statement: Four checks fail mutually independently, each with probability \(1/4\). X counts the failed checks.
cs-u19-q01.prompt: What is the probability that X equals 1?
cs-u19-q01.hint: There are four choices for which check fails.
cs-u19-q01.explanation: \(P(X=1)=\binom{4}{1}(1/4)(3/4)^3=27/64\). The single-path probability \(27/256\) omits the other three possible failed checks.
solutionSteps: \(P(X=1)=\binom{4}{1}(1/4)(3/4)^3=27/64\). The single-path probability \(27/256\) omits the other three possible failed checks.

cs-u19-q02.title: Recover the probability at one value
cs-u19-q02.statement: R is an integer-valued retry count. Its CDF satisfies \(F_R(3)=0.60\) and \(F_R(4)=0.85\).
cs-u19-q02.prompt: What is the probability that R equals 4? Enter a decimal.
cs-u19-q02.hint: Remove the probability of values at most 3 from the probability of values at most 4.
cs-u19-q02.explanation: \(P(R=4)=F_R(4)-F_R(3)=0.85-0.60=0.25\). The integer-valued assumption ensures there are no possible values strictly between 3 and 4.
solutionSteps: \(P(R=4)=F_R(4)-F_R(3)=0.85-0.60=0.25\). The integer-valued assumption ensures there are no possible values strictly between 3 and 4.

cs-u19-q03.title: Expected occupied buckets
cs-u19-q03.statement: Three distinct keys hash independently and uniformly into four buckets. O is the number of buckets containing at least one key.
cs-u19-q03.prompt: What is the expected value of O?
cs-u19-q03.hint: For one fixed bucket, compute the probability that all three keys miss it.
cs-u19-q03.explanation: A fixed bucket is occupied with probability \(1-(3/4)^3=37/64\). Summing four bucket indicators gives \(E[O]=4(37/64)=37/16\). The occupancy indicators are dependent, but linearity still applies.
solutionSteps: A fixed bucket is occupied with probability \(1-(3/4)^3=37/64\). Summing four bucket indicators gives \(E[O]=4(37/64)=37/16\). The occupancy indicators are dependent, but linearity still applies.

cs-u19-q04.title: Count adjacent descents without independence
cs-u19-q04.statement: A scheduler uniformly shuffles tasks with distinct IDs 1 through 8. D counts adjacent positions where the left ID is larger than the right ID.
cs-u19-q04.prompt: What is the expected value of D? Enter a decimal.
cs-u19-q04.hint: There are seven adjacent pairs of positions. By symmetry, each is a descent with probability one half.
cs-u19-q04.explanation: Write D as the sum of seven descent indicators. Swapping the IDs in a fixed pair of positions shows that its descent probability is \(1/2\). Thus \(E[D]=7/2=3.5\). Overlapping pair indicators need not be independent.
