cs-u19-q05.title: Expected time with unlimited retries
cs-u19-q05.statement: Independent attempts succeed with probability \(1/4\). Each attempt takes exactly 2 ms, whether it succeeds or fails. Retry until the first success; there is no other overhead.
cs-u19-q05.prompt: What is the expected total time, in milliseconds?
cs-u19-q05.hint: Let T be the expected time. The first attempt costs 2 ms; after a failure the same problem restarts.
cs-u19-q05.explanation: \(T=2+(3/4)T\), so \(T=8\) ms. Equivalently, the expected number of attempts is 4 and each costs 2 ms. The successful attempt is included.
solutionSteps: \(T=2+(3/4)T\), so \(T=8\) ms. Equivalently, the expected number of attempts is 4 and each costs 2 ms. The successful attempt is included.

cs-u19-q06.title: Do not use the unlimited-retry mean after a cap
cs-u19-q06.statement: Independent attempts succeed with probability 0.5. Stop at the first success or after three attempts, whichever occurs first. N counts attempts actually made.
cs-u19-q06.prompt: What is the expected value of N? Enter a decimal.
cs-u19-q06.hint: Attempt 1 always occurs, attempt 2 requires one failure, and attempt 3 requires two failures.
cs-u19-q06.explanation: \(E[N]=1+1/2+1/4=7/4=1.75\). Equivalently, \(P(N=1)=1/2\), \(P(N=2)=1/4\) and \(P(N=3)=1/4\). The last case includes both success and failure on attempt 3.
solutionSteps: \(E[N]=1+1/2+1/4=7/4=1.75\). Equivalently, \(P(N=1)=1/2\), \(P(N=2)=1/4\) and \(P(N=3)=1/4\). The last case includes both success and failure on attempt 3.

cs-u20-q01.title: A latency guarantee from its mean
cs-u20-q01.statement: Latency T is nonnegative and \(E[T]=12\) ms. No other distribution information is available.
cs-u20-q01.prompt: What upper bound does Markov give for latency at least 60 ms? Enter a decimal.
cs-u20-q01.hint: Divide the mean by the threshold.
cs-u20-q01.explanation: \(P(T\ge60)\le12/60=0.2\). This bound can be attained by a distribution with T = 60 with probability 0.2 and T = 0 otherwise; the mean alone cannot give a smaller universal bound.
solutionSteps: \(P(T\ge60)\le12/60=0.2\). This bound can be attained by a distribution with T = 60 with probability 0.2 and T = 0 otherwise; the mean alone cannot give a smaller universal bound.

cs-u20-q02.title: A two-sided deviation bound
cs-u20-q02.statement: A counter X has \(E[X]=100\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(X)=9\). Its distribution is otherwise unspecified.
cs-u20-q02.hint: Divide the variance by the square of the deviation threshold, 6.
cs-u20-q02.explanation: \(P(|X-100|\ge6)\le9/6^2=1/4\). This is an upper bound; the probability need not equal it. No Gaussian assumption is supplied or needed.
solutionSteps: \(P(|X-100|\ge6)\le9/6^2=1/4\). This is an upper bound; the probability need not equal it. No Gaussian assumption is supplied or needed.

cs-u20-q03.title: Copying a measurement adds no precision
cs-u20-q03.statement: A measurement X has variance 9. A program copies this same realized value into four rows and computes \(Z=(X+X+X+X)/4\).
cs-u20-q03.prompt: What is the variance of Z?
cs-u20-q03.hint: Simplify the random variable Z before using a variance formula.
cs-u20-q03.explanation: \(Z=X\) for every outcome, so \(\operatorname{Var}(Z)=9\). The four rows are identical copies, not independent measurements; dividing 9 by 4 would be unjustified.
solutionSteps: \(Z=X\) for every outcome, so \(\operatorname{Var}(Z)=9\). The four rows are identical copies, not independent measurements; dividing 9 by 4 would be unjustified.

cs-u20-q04.title: Size a conservative Bernoulli sample
cs-u20-q04.statement: \(X_1,\ldots,X_n\) are pairwise independent Bernoulli(p) observations with unknown common p. Use the bound \(P(|\bar X-p|\ge0.05)\le1/(4n(0.05)^2)\).
cs-u20-q04.prompt: What is the smallest integer n making this bound at most 0.05?
cs-u20-q04.explanation: The bound equals \(100/n\), so \(100/n\le0.05\) requires \(n\ge2000\). This is the minimum certified by this conservative bound, not a claim that every estimation method needs 2000 observations.
solutionSteps: The bound equals \(100/n\), so \(100/n\le0.05\) requires \(n\ge2000\). This is the minimum certified by this conservative bound, not a claim that every estimation method needs 2000 observations.

cs-u20-q05.title: Bound a high failure count
cs-u20-q05.statement: There are 200 mutually independent checks, each failing with probability 0.05. S counts failures.
cs-u20-q05.prompt: Which upper bound follows from the stated Chernoff formula for at least 20 failures?
cs-u20-q05.hint: Compute the mean, then the threshold divided by that mean.
cs-u20-q05.explanation: \(\mu=200(0.05)=10\) and \(c=20/10=2\). Hence \(P(S\ge20)\le\exp(-10(2\ln2-1))=(e/4)^{10}\). This is a bound, not an exact binomial tail probability.
solutionSteps: \(\mu=200(0.05)=10\) and \(c=20/10=2\). Hence \(P(S\ge20)\le\exp(-10(2\ln2-1))=(e/4)^{10}\). This is a bound, not an exact binomial tail probability.

cs-u20-q06.title: Reject a bound on cloned indicators
cs-u20-q06.statement: One Bernoulli variable B equals 1 with probability 0.1. Set \(X_1=\cdots=X_{100}=B\) and \(S=\sum_iX_i\). Someone uses \(E[S]=10\) to claim \(P(S\ge20)\le(e/4)^{10}\).
cs-u20-q06.prompt: Why is that use of Chernoff invalid?
cs-u20-q06.hint: All 100 summands change together. What is the actual event that S is at least 20?
cs-u20-q06.explanation: The summands are not mutually independent. In fact \(S=100B\), so \(P(S\ge20)=0.1\), exceeding \((e/4)^{10}\approx0.021\). Correct bounds on individual summands and the correct mean do not replace the independence assumption.
solutionSteps: The summands are not mutually independent. In fact \(S=100B\), so \(P(S\ge20)=0.1\), exceeding \((e/4)^{10}\approx0.021\). Correct bounds on individual summands and the correct mean do not replace the independence assumption.

options.a: The summands are identical copies and are not mutually independent.
options.b: The summands take values outside the interval [0,1].
options.c: Their sum has mean 100 rather than 10.

cs-u21-q01.title: A fair walk need not give a 50/50 outcome
cs-u21-q01.statement: A walk starts at 3 and stops on reaching 0 or 12. Each step independently moves +1 or -1 with equal probability.
cs-u21-q01.prompt: What is the probability of reaching 12 first? Enter a decimal.
cs-u21-q01.hint: The step direction is fair, but the starting point is not halfway between the boundaries.
cs-u21-q01.explanation: For the fair walk, \(h_i=i/N\), so \(h_3=3/12=0.25\). Equal step probabilities do not make unequally distant absorbing boundaries equally likely.
solutionSteps: For the fair walk, \(h_i=i/N\), so \(h_3=3/12=0.25\). Equal step probabilities do not make unequally distant absorbing boundaries equally likely.

cs-u21-q02.title: Solve a small biased walk
cs-u21-q02.statement: A walk starts at 1 and stops at 0 or 3. Each step independently moves +1 with probability \(1/3\) and -1 with probability \(2/3\).
cs-u21-q02.prompt: What is the probability of reaching 3 first?
cs-u21-q02.explanation: Substitution gives \(h_1=1/9+(2/9)h_1\), hence \(h_1=1/7\). The general formula agrees: \(r=2\) and \((1-2)/(1-2^3)=1/7\).
solutionSteps: Substitution gives \(h_1=1/9+(2/9)h_1\), hence \(h_1=1/7\). The general formula agrees: \(r=2\) and \((1-2)/(1-2^3)=1/7\).

cs-u21-q03.title: Include the final step into a boundary
cs-u21-q03.statement: A walk starts at 2 and stops at 0 or 7. Each step independently moves +1 or -1 with equal probability. Count every step up to absorption.
cs-u21-q03.prompt: What is the expected number of steps?
cs-u21-q03.hint: Use the initial distance to each boundary in the fair-walk formula.
cs-u21-q03.explanation: \(e_2=2(7-2)=10\). This is an average over paths ending at either boundary; it is not merely the distance to the nearer one.
solutionSteps: \(e_2=2(7-2)=10\). This is an average over paths ending at either boundary; it is not merely the distance to the nearer one.

cs-u21-q04.title: Infinite mean does not mean never stopping
cs-u21-q04.statement: A fair walk starts at 1 on the nonnegative integers and stops at 0. Steps are independent; there is no upper boundary.
cs-u21-q04.hint: Compare with walks stopped at 0 or N, and let N grow.
cs-u21-q04.explanation: The chance of reaching 0 is at least \(1-1/N\) for every N, so it is 1. The unbounded hitting time is at least the time to reach 0 or N, whose mean from 1 is \(N-1\). Its mean is therefore infinite, even though it is finite with probability 1.
solutionSteps: The chance of reaching 0 is at least \(1-1/N\) for every N, so it is 1. The unbounded hitting time is at least the time to reach 0 or N, whose mean from 1 is \(N-1\). Its mean is therefore infinite, even though it is finite with probability 1.

options.a: It reaches 0 with probability 1 and has a finite expected hitting time.
options.b: Infinite expected time means a positive probability of never reaching 0.
options.c: It reaches 0 with probability 1 but has infinite expected hitting time.

cs-u21-q05.title: Balance flow on a three-vertex graph
cs-u21-q05.statement: The only directed edges are \(A\to B\), \(A\to C\), \(B\to A\), \(C\to A\). At each step choose an outgoing edge uniformly.
cs-u21-q05.prompt: Which probability vector, in the order (A,B,C), is stationary?
cs-u21-q05.hint: A sends half its probability to each leaf; both leaves send all their probability to A.
cs-u21-q05.explanation: Stationarity requires \(\pi_B=\pi_A/2\), \(\pi_C=\pi_A/2\) and \(\pi_A=\pi_B+\pi_C\). Normalization gives \(2\pi_A=1\), hence \((1/2,1/4,1/4)\). Substitution verifies the one-step balance.
solutionSteps: Stationarity requires \(\pi_B=\pi_A/2\), \(\pi_C=\pi_A/2\) and \(\pi_A=\pi_B+\pi_C\). Normalization gives \(2\pi_A=1\), hence \((1/2,1/4,1/4)\). Substitution verifies the one-step balance.

cs-u21-q06.title: A unique stationary distribution is not enough
cs-u21-q06.statement: The only edges are \(A\to B\), \(A\to C\), \(B\to A\), \(C\to A\), with uniform outgoing choices. Start at A with probability 1. The stationary distribution is \((1/2,1/4,1/4)\).
cs-u21-q06.prompt: Does the distribution at step t converge to that stationary distribution?
cs-u21-q06.hint: Track the probability of being at A at even and odd times.
cs-u21-q06.explanation: At even times the distribution is \((1,0,0)\); at odd times it is \((0,1/2,1/2)\). It does not converge. Flow balance describes what happens when initialized at stationarity, not what every starting distribution must approach.
solutionSteps: At even times the distribution is \((1,0,0)\); at odd times it is \((0,1/2,1/2)\). It does not converge. Flow balance describes what happens when initialized at stationarity, not what every starting distribution must approach.

options.a: Yes: existence of a unique stationary distribution guarantees convergence.
options.b: No: the distribution alternates between two different vectors.
options.c: No: the displayed stationary distribution fails to sum to 1.

cs-u22-q01.title: Count the complete recursion tree
cs-u22-q01.statement: A call at depth \(n>0\) executes two calls at depth \(n-1\), then exactly 3 local operations. A depth-0 call costs 1 operation. Both calls execute fully; no results are reused. These are the only counted operations.
cs-u22-q01.prompt: How many operations does one depth-4 call perform?
cs-u22-q01.hint: Use \(T_0=1\) and \(T_n=2T_{n-1}+3\), or count internal calls and leaves separately.
cs-u22-q01.explanation: There are \(2^4=16\) leaves and \(1+2+4+8=15\) internal calls. The total is \(16+3(15)=61\). Equivalently, the recurrence gives 1, 5, 13, 29, 61. Following only one branch would miss most of the work.
solutionSteps: There are \(2^4=16\) leaves and \(1+2+4+8=15\) internal calls. The total is \(16+3(15)=61\). Equivalently, the recurrence gives 1, 5, 13, 29, 61. Following only one branch would miss most of the work.

cs-u22-q02.title: Strengthen a bound so the proof closes
cs-u22-q02.statement: Let \(T_0=1\) and \(T_n=2T_{n-1}+3\) for \(n\ge1\). Trying to prove \(T_n\le4\cdot2^n\) by substitution gives only \(T_n\le4\cdot2^n+3\).
cs-u22-q02.prompt: Which bound satisfies the base case and closes the inductive step?
cs-u22-q02.hint: For a candidate \(T_n\le4\cdot2^n-c\), check both \(1\le4-c\) and the effect of doubling the previous bound and adding 3.
cs-u22-q02.explanation: With c = 3, the base bound is \(1\le4-3=1\). The step gives \(2(4\cdot2^{n-1}-3)+3=4\cdot2^n-3\). Choice A still leaves excess overhead after substitution; choice C fails at n = 0. A failed proof of the original bound does not make that bound false.
solutionSteps: With c = 3, the base bound is \(1\le4-3=1\). The step gives \(2(4\cdot2^{n-1}-3)+3=4\cdot2^n-3\). Choice A still leaves excess overhead after substitution; choice C fails at n = 0. A failed proof of the original bound does not make that bound false.

cs-u22-q03.title: The largest root can disappear
cs-u22-q03.statement: A sequence satisfies \(f_0=1\), \(f_1=2\), and \(f_n=5f_{n-1}-6f_{n-2}\) for \(n\ge2\). Its characteristic roots are 2 and 3.
cs-u22-q03.prompt: What is the tight asymptotic growth of this sequence?
cs-u22-q03.hint: Write \(f_n=A2^n+B3^n\) and use both initial values.
cs-u22-q03.explanation: The initial values give \(A+B=1\) and \(2A+3B=2\), hence A = 1 and B = 0. Thus \(f_n=2^n\) and its growth is \(\Theta(2^n)\). The largest characteristic root does not contribute because its coefficient vanishes.
solutionSteps: The initial values give \(A+B=1\) and \(2A+3B=2\), hence A = 1 and B = 0. Thus \(f_n=2^n\) and its growth is \(\Theta(2^n)\). The largest characteristic root does not contribute because its coefficient vanishes.

cs-u22-q04.title: Keep the repeated-root term
cs-u22-q04.statement: A sequence satisfies \(f_0=1\), \(f_1=6\), and \(f_n=6f_{n-1}-9f_{n-2}\) for \(n\ge2\). Its characteristic polynomial is \((r-3)^2\).
cs-u22-q04.prompt: Which formula satisfies the recurrence and both initial values?
cs-u22-q04.hint: The double root gives \(f_n=(A+Bn)3^n\); solve for A and B.
cs-u22-q04.explanation: The initial values imply A = 1 and \(3(A+B)=6\), so B = 1. Hence \(f_n=(n+1)3^n\). All three choices match the two initial values, but at n = 2 the recurrence requires \(6(6)-9(1)=27\); choices B and C give 36 and 21.
solutionSteps: The initial values imply A = 1 and \(3(A+B)=6\), so B = 1. Hence \(f_n=(n+1)3^n\). All three choices match the two initial values, but at n = 2 the recurrence requires \(6(6)-9(1)=27\); choices B and C give 36 and 21.

cs-u22-q05.title: Four half-size calls change the growth
cs-u22-q05.statement: For powers of two \(n\ge2\), an algorithm has \(T(1)=1\) and \(T(n)=4T(n/2)+n\). All four calls execute fully; no results are reused.
cs-u22-q05.prompt: What is the tight asymptotic running time?
cs-u22-q05.hint: At level j, multiply \(4^j\) calls by their local cost \(n/2^j\). Also count the leaves.
cs-u22-q05.explanation: Level j costs \(n2^j\), so later levels are more expensive. There are \(4^{\log_2 n}=n^2\) unit-cost leaves. Internal work sums to \(n(n-1)\); total work is \(2n^2-n=\Theta(n^2)\). Halving the size alone does not guarantee Merge Sort's growth rate.
solutionSteps: Level j costs \(n2^j\), so later levels are more expensive. There are \(4^{\log_2 n}=n^2\) unit-cost leaves. Internal work sums to \(n(n-1)\); total work is \(2n^2-n=\Theta(n^2)\). Halving the size alone does not guarantee Merge Sort's growth rate.

cs-u22-q06.title: An extra logarithm in the combine step
cs-u22-q06.statement: A recursive algorithm has \(T(1)=1\) and \(T(n)=2T(n/2)+n\log_2 n\) for powers of two \(n\ge2\).
cs-u22-q06.prompt: What is the tight asymptotic running time?
cs-u22-q06.hint: Let \(k=\log_2 n\). The combined local work at level j is \(n(k-j)\); sum for \(j=0,\ldots,k-1\).
cs-u22-q06.explanation: The internal levels cost \(n(k+(k-1)+\cdots+1)=nk(k+1)/2\). Adding n leaves gives \(T(n)=n(1+k(k+1)/2)=\Theta(n(\log_2 n)^2)\). The extra logarithmic work at each call changes the overall bound.
solutionSteps: The internal levels cost \(n(k+(k-1)+\cdots+1)=nk(k+1)/2\). Adding n leaves gives \(T(n)=n(1+k(k+1)/2)=\Theta(n(\log_2 n)^2)\). The extra logarithmic work at each call changes the overall bound.
